subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECRUITMENT OF PERSONNEL FOR QUEBEC OFFICE
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECRUITMENT OF PERSONNEL FOR QUEBEC OFFICE
speechtext:
1.	Does the Quebec office of the Post Office Department recruit staff through competition or personal interview?
2.	If by competition are they public or simply reserved for a small group?

subtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-RECRUITMENT OF PERSONNEL FOR QUEBEC OFFICE
speechtext:
1. The
Quebec postal region recruits its staff by open competition. Candidates are expected to fill out an application form which is subsequently studied by a personnel officer. If the candidate claims to possess the required qualifications and he passes the written examination, in cases where such is a requirement, he will be called for interview by a selection board. The personal interview, therefore, is an integral part of the competition process. No employee is admitted to permanent status within the Department who has not been interviewed. I must add, however, that the Quebec postal region, in common with departmental practice across Canada, does not necessarily resort to open competition when filling positions for which there are adequate candidates within the department. This applies to nearly all supervisory or promotion positions, and for certain lower level positions which are filled from the ranks of casual or part-time employees. A personal interview would not necessarily be held, for instance, if a part-time employee, who was well known to the supervisor, was moved into a permanent position. He would, however, have been interviewed when first recruited as a part-time employee.
2. There are no restrictions as to who may or may not apply in an open competition.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. I. Benson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: POLICING BY ARMED FORCES FOR ARCTIC POLLUTION CONTROL
speechtext:
1. The
Department of National Defence has been engaged actively in an anti-pollution campaign in the Arctic for the past several years. Most of the activities have been carried out with other federal departments who have jurisdiction in the area. The main pollution problem is litter and debris. In 1970, air support was provided to Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to carry out reconnaissance of four abandoned Distant Early Warning sites. In 1971, this program was continued to include an additional 12 sites. The reconnaissance of the five remaining sites which are located on Baffin Island will be carried out during the summer of 1972. Air reserve squadrons have assisted in these reconnaissance and pollution survey missions. As a result of the findings from these reconnaissance flights, a cleanup of Stokes Point. Y.T., is scheduled for July 1972. This will be a combined operation between DND and DIAND and will serve as a pilot project to determine the financial and manpower requirements for the clean-up of the other sites. The Department of Environment is scheduled to carry out an inspection of selected active DEW line sites this summer to ascertain conditions at these locations. At Canadian Forces' Station Alert, a work party and a drum crusher will eliminate pollution from discarded oil drums. A sanitary landfill operation also will be put into operation to alleviate the solid waste disposal problem. Garbage emanating from exercises and manoeuvres in the north is transported out for proper disposal.
2. No members of the Canadian Armed Forces are maintained in the Arctic for the specific purpose of policing (a) the pollution control zone (b) the new fisheries closing line. However, Mobile Command long range patrol aircraft when flying over the Arctic report pollution and fishing control zone violations.

speechtext: In view of the fact this is taking place despite the deficit on current account and the falling off in our trading position, and in view of the fact the main reason for the increase in the level of our dollar seems to be the inflow of short-term money resulting from the differential between our short-term interest rates and other short-term interest rates, can the minister give us any information as to the volume of the inflow of shortterm money coming into Canada?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN DOLLAR EXCHANGE LEVEL-MEASURES TO REDUCE SHORT-TERM CAPITAL INFLOW-ASSISTANCE TO EXPORTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is quite right that if one were to take the current account alone, which has fallen off from a surplus position, one might draw one's conclusions as to the exchange rate. But aside from the general weakness of the U.S. dollar, which has made that problem a universal one, there are two situations in Canada affecting the Canadian dollar particularly, and about which I have been concerned.
One has to do with the amount of current borrowing for long-term funds by the provinces on foreign markets. The other has to do with a strong demand by the Canadian banks for short-term capital, short-term money, in order to relieve their liquidity problems. I might say that on that latter subject I had some discussion with the Canadian Bankers Association when I was in Winnipeg on Thursday night.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN DOLLAR EXCHANGE LEVEL-MEASURES TO REDUCE SHORT-TERM CAPITAL INFLOW-ASSISTANCE TO EXPORTERS
speechtext: Am I to infer from the final sentence in the minister's answer that he has suggested some guidelines to the banks with regard to the borrowing of shortterm funds from abroad?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN DOLLAR EXCHANGE LEVEL-MEASURES TO REDUCE SHORT-TERM CAPITAL INFLOW-ASSISTANCE TO EXPORTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I spoke to representatives of the Canadian banks on the occasion of the annual meeting of the Canadian Bankers Association in Winnipeg last Thursday. During the course of my remarks I said we were concerned about rates of interest and the exchange value of the Canadian dollar.
I have now received from the president of the Canadian Bankers Association a request that I approve an agreement among the banks that will have the effect of reducing the rates paid by banks on their larger certificates of deposit, that is to say, street deposits maturing within one year. I have already indicated my approval in principle of this agreement under section 138 of the Bank Act because in my view it will contribute to the objectives of the government in the field of finance affecting interest rates and in the realm of foreign exchange.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN DOLLAR EXCHANGE LEVEL-MEASURES TO REDUCE SHORT-TERM CAPITAL INFLOW-ASSISTANCE TO EXPORTERS
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister whether it is the position of the government to permit the Canadian dollar to remain at this level or whether the minister is considering measures to assist our producers and exporters in the event that this condition continues?

speakeroldname: Hon. lames Richardson (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the budget debate, the fifth day, most of the facts, figures and policies have been examined and discussed by both sides of the House. My purpose in entering the debate at this time is to elaborate on one sentence in the budget speech, a sentence that I consider to be important above all others. Also, I particularly want to enter the debate at this time so that I can speak about the purchasing policies of the federal government, the policies of my department, as they relate to that sentence in the budget speech.
Along with what else the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said on May 8 were these words:
National unity has a great deal to do with equality of opportunity-equality of opportunity for Canadians, no matter where they happen to be born or where they happen to live in our country.
The kind of equality of opportunity I will talk about is equality of opportunity for Canadians from coast to coast who want to sell their manufactured goods and their services to their federal government; in other words, those who want to sell to the national government. I believe hon. members know the Department of Supply and Services is a purchasing department and also an accounting department. I have often said that had we been called the purchasing department and the accounting department of government, more Canadian citizens would know what we do. In fact, however, we do more than that. We do many more things. We are responsible for materiel management, for warehousing, for the disposal of equipment and also the provision of management consulting services, as well as the provision of complex computer services.
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
Therefore, because we do more than simply purchasing and accounting we have been given, in someone's wisdom, the somewhat obscure title of Supply and Services.
The aspect of our operation about which I want to speak particularly today is purchasing, because the department is one of the largest purchasing organizations in Canada. As it buys more than $1 billion worth of goods and services each year, its operations affect the lives, particularly the business lives, of many Canadian companies large and small. We make purchases from literally thousands of Canadian companies. On behalf of other government departments, we are busy each day buying everything from pencil sharpeners to the largest computers, everything from toothpaste to the most advanced and modern aircraft.
When I first began to look over the vast amount of purchasing undertaken for the federal government through my department I was surprised-and I may say as a western Canadian I was somewhat amazed and under some circumstances annoyed-to find the extent to which federal government purchasing was concentrated in a relatively small region of Canada, a region not more than 300 miles from the national capital, in a country 4,000 miles wide. When I looked at the figures, I found out that year in and year out more than 85 per cent of federal government purchases were made in the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It did not seem to me that figures such as these were consistent with equality of opportunity for Canadians. I am therefore pleased to have this occasion to tell the House that for some time now we have been in the process of evolving purchasing policies which will help correct this concentration of purchasing and will give Canadians from coast to coast a greater opportunity to sell to their national government.
When Canadians are selling to the federal government they are, of course, selling to themselves because as taxpayers in a sense they are both buyers and sellers. In what I am saying today I want to emphasize that I am talking about an evolving purchasing policy. I am talking about something that is partly in place and in operation, and partly in the process of formation. That which is still in the process of formation constitutes goals or objectives rather than established policy.
The policy I am now developing within the department has three main characteristics or three main parts. The first part, which is still in the nature of an objective, is that we propose to establish federal government purchasing targets within four large regions of Canada. These targets would be based roughly upon the population in each region. For this purpose, the regions must be large because obviously we want to have competition within the regions. If we selected one small province and tried to localize buying in that province we would not have the competition necessary to obtain the lowest price. Therefore the regions for which we want to establish targets within the department are four. The first area is the Atlantic provinces region which I think of for this purpose as Canada East. Quebec is one region and Ontario is one region. The four provinces in the west for this purpose, and also for some other purposes from time to time, I call Canada West.

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
If we examine the figures for federal government purchasing which has actually taken place over the past six years, we find that under 6 per cent of all purchases have been made in the four Atlantic provinces. We find that over 40 per cent of these purchases have been made in Quebec, some 44 per cent in Ontario and under 10 per cent in the region of Canada West. When we consider establishing targets based on the population of these regions, we find that the Atlantic provinces contain almost 10 per cent of the Canadian population, Quebec approximately 28 per cent, Ontario 35 per cent and Canada West 27 per cent. Comparing the number of Canadians in each of these four regions with the amount they have been able to sell to their national government we find that in Canada West 27 per cent of the population receives under 10 per cent of federal government purchases. In the Atlantic provinces, 10 per cent of the national population has been receiving less than 6 per cent of federal purchases. In Quebec, we find 28 per cent of the national population and more than 40 per cent of the national purchases. In Ontario, we find 35 per cent of the population and some 44 per cent of the purchases. These figures do not cover just the last week or month but are averages over the last six years.
In other words, the story is quite clear. The federal government which after all is a national government, a coast-to-coast government, does not buy in equal measure or in anything approaching equal measure from all the citizens and taxpayers of the country. I do not believe it would be practical to make a hard and fast rule requiring that federal government purchases meet established targets in each region. However, I should like to see our purchasing policy so ordered that federal buying in each of these four regions, would, in percentage terms at least, approach the populations of those regions. Our first objective is to establish targets.
The second characteristic of this evolving policy-and this part in fact is now being implemented and is policy- is to increase the amount of purchasing done through our regional offices. Last year for those who may be interested in the total figures we purchased $178 million of government requirements through the regional offices, while $897 million was spent on what we call national purchases made from Ottawa. Members of the House will appreciate that we can reach the kind of fair regional balance that I am talking about in one of two ways. We can either increase the amount of regional buying that is done from the centre or we can increase the buying that is done through the regional offices. Those are two distinct operations, but they both have the effect of increasing regional buying.
There is a clear advantage to more regional buying, which is that when we purchase through regional offices, in most cases we have a substantial cut in the distribution costs of the goods purchased, particularly when they are required in the area in which the purchase is made. As well, in order to increase the regional buying we have been actively seeking new sources of supply, that is we have been looking for companies across Canada which have never before sold to the federal government. This is just "good business" so far as the government is con-

cerned, because of course the more suppliers we have the more competition we can have among suppliers. I think the House will be interested to know that a number of businesses that have never before sold to the federal government are now receiving orders. These are orders and contracts that are open to tender and are awarded to the lowest bidder.
Looking for a moment at some specific areas in the purchasing field, may I point out that it is encouraging to see that the amount of federal government printing business, awarded in this case, in the prairie provinces during six months, that is during the half year ending March 1972, exceeded the total of printing business that companies on the Prairies received during the whole of the previous year. I should like to point out also that in the Atlantic provinces we have been successful in encouraging the development of marine technology, and substantial purchases of marine equipment have been made in that region. Still another example is the government's furniture requirements which used to be purchased centrally and then distributed to all parts of the country with relatively high distribution costs. I have already reported to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee that a major part of the federal government's furniture requirements in western Canada, not their total furniture requirements but the furniture required in western Canada, has now been won under competition by western Canadian firms, and this furniture is now being manufactured in western Canada.
Still speaking about regional purchases, I am encouraged to be able to report that the purchases in our regional offices in western Canada increased by 21 per cent in the last fiscal year over the previous year. In the case of the Atlantic provinces, the percentage increase was even higher and amounted to 27 per cent over the previous year. In looking at these percentage increases, encouraging as they are, it is of course necessary to realize that the western and Atlantic regions started from a very low base and there is still a long way to go to achieve equality of opportunity or even to approach the regional targets mentioned earlier.
Finally, the third and most important characteristic of federal government purchasing which I think should be considered relates to the cost of transportation. It is apparent to everyone that in a country of vast distances there are many companies that are a long way from the destination where the goods are required and thus are prevented from bidding effectively because of transportation costs. A proposal which I intend to discuss further with my colleages is the establishment of a policy under which any Canadian who wishes to sell to his national government can bid on the basis of his costs at his plant, that is his bid will be judged f.o.b. plant rather than f.o.b. destination which would of course then include transportation costs to destination. This proposed policy would be one way to demonstrate clearly that as the national government we really mean what we say when we talk about equality of opportunity for Canadians in all parts of Canada.
Before speaking further on that aspect of our policy, I should like to refer to a speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made in my home city of Winnipeg a few
June 12, 1972

days ago on May 26. I need hardly say that he was speaking to a crowded audience.

No, at any time. It would seem to me to be very consistent with that concept if we were able to say to all Canadians when you sell to your government you can compete with each other based on the costs in your own plant and upon your own efficiency, but so far as transportation costs in this land of great distances are concerned, every one of you can sell to the national government in the same way as you could if you happened to live near Parliament Hill. The government of course cannot eliminate inefficiency within a business, and in that sense all Canadians cannot bid equally-some are clearly more efficient than others, and it is to the benefit of our whole economy that they are. But we can do something about eliminating the disparity of distance, and it is in that direction that I hope to continue to move our purchasing policies.
I should emphasize that nothing in this suggestion-and this is for anyone who may be concerned about the big plants in this region or in any other region of Canada- would be harmful to any manufacturer anywhere in Canada. No one anywhere would be put at a disadvantage. The largest plants in the heavily industrialized regions of Canada would of course still retain the advantage of size and the advantage of whatever efficiency they have attained as well as the continuing advantage of proximity to the national capital and to the national buying offices of the government. Of course, they would also retain some advantage in the cost of their inward freight. It is important to realize, for instance, that a printer in western Canada, even if he is able to bid f.o.b. his plant and therefore has no transportation cost on the finished product, still has to move the bulk paper into his plant before he can bid against a company that does not have to move its raw materials the same distance.
The Budget-Mr. Richardson
In summary, Mr. Speaker, what I have been talking about is the desirability of moving further towards federal government purchasing policies that will increase equality of opportunity for Canadians from coast to coast, equality of opportunity for Canadians who wish to sell to the national government. I have talked about the establishment of federal government purchasing targets for each of the four large regions in Canada. I have talked about increasing the volume of federal purchasing through regional offices, and I have mentioned the progress we have made in that direction. Third, I have said that it would be fair play if anyone who wishes to sell to the federal government were able to have his bid judged according to the costs in his own plant, and not judged on the cost at destination. I am convinced that these policies in combination will help to achieve the goal of equality of opportunity. It seems only right to me that national purchases should bring about nationwide economic benefits.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should respond briefly to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who made a contribution to the budget debate several days ago. He made his usual worthwhile contribution, and mentioned-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris made a number of comments, and first I would like to thank him for some of his references to my efforts to try to explain the aspirations of western Canada, many of which he has outlined himself. In particular, he mentioned a seminar which was held in his home city of Brandon. It was a two-day seminar and was a very successful one at which I had the honour to be a guest panellist. We talked all day, and I am afraid a few of us talked most of the night. We covered a lot of ground, and it would be impossible to give the conclusion which the hon. member has requested. I wish he had been there because it was a non-partisan occasion throughout which his colleague, the able young member for Lisgar, attended.
If I tried to say in a sentence what that seminar concluded, as I have been asked to do, I would say to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris that western Canadians concluded that what the west wants is a greater participation in industrialization, in scientific, technological, advanced, economic endeavour. What happens is that the west has a tremendous agricultural base, a tremendous resource base, a tremendous energy base. But as long as it concentrates on policies for those, important as they are, it still is a hinterland of a sort. It still has a very adverse balance of trade, of manufacturing trade, with the eastern provinces of Canada.
So really the issue which was faced in those two days, and resolved, was that in western Canada we must build an advanced society on top of the agricultural base, and on top of the energy base, and on top of the mining

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Richardson resource base. That is the point that has to be clarified, because we all spend a good deal of time talking about the agricultural requirements of the west. And they are important, Mr. Speaker, but we could sell not just a billion bushels, we could sell two billion bushels of wheat and we still would not have answered the needs of western Canadians who are going to university in Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg and, of course, Brandon. These young people are not in university so that they can be wheat farmers. They are there because they want to be designers, engineers, and computer technicians. That is the requirement and that was the conclusion.
How we are to achieve this was also concluded at that meeting, and again I will try to put it in two sentences. It is in one of two ways. Clearly, the west must achieve greater influence at the centre. We can either have a strong central government in which there is a strong regional voice-obviously this would be comparable to the American central government and its decentralized space program and other programs-or the alternative has to be, in a federation, to increase the influence of the provinces or the regional governments, if they become regional governments. Those are the alternatives, and I think that at the present time we are making headway in the first direction. We are achieving some decentralization. We are achieving some of the west's requirement for participation in the economic endeavours of the nation, in major programs like the aerospace program. But these have still to be proven as we go down the road. We will have to see in the future if the west participates in these great national programs in the way it must before we determine which of those answers we finally choose in order to achieve the obvious potential of that region.
That is a very quick summary, Mr. Speaker, but I felt that as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris had called on me at least three or four times during his address, I should try to respond briefly, although it was not the main theme of my speech today.

So, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance was not addressing himself to the purchasing policies that I have been describing, but I am encouraged by the central theme of his budget address.
I think that I may say in conclusion that all of us who were in the House on the evening of May 8 listening to the Minister of Finance recognized immediately that Canada could be standing on the threshhold of a new era. We realized that we were listening not only to a new man at the helm of the vital Department of Finance but also that we were listening to a new definition and a clearer understanding of the all-important relationship that must exist, in a free society, between the men who run the government of the day and the men who manage the large and the small business enterprises of the nation. I am convinced, as I know the Minister of Finance is, that it is the degree of confidence which business and government have in each other that will ultimately determine the economic success of our whole society. The Minister of Finance's budget has taken us farther toward the achieve-

ment of that mutual confidence than any single document in recent time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opportunity to take part in this budget debate is one which I deeply appreciate. This particular budget, Mr. Speaker, is a long one. It tries to do many things and, although we in the opposition may have some unkind things to say about it, none of us, I am sure, wants to see the measures taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) fail, simply so that we can say, in effect, we told you so. Rather, we are optimistic that what has been done by the hon. minister is a step, or even several steps, in the right direction. However, Mr. Speaker, we would all be remiss in our duties as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition if we did not bring to the attention of the government things which should have been done and benefits which could have been realized through policies that would aid Canadians in general.
This budget finally concedes that it is from the private sector of our economy that the thrust of our economic development must come. It is only from the private sector that we can get the necessary energy and resources to expand our nation. All the best intentioned academics, theoriticians and civil servants, and for that matter politicians, ultimately cannot be anything more than spectators who, in the final analysis, can only exhort the individual members of the private sector of our economy to help us realize our potential. Hopefully, the Minister of Finance will seek advice in formulating our economic policies from people with practical experience instead of relying, as I feel this government has done in the past, on the advice of people long on theory and short on practice.
June 12, 1972

The hon. Minister of Finance, while adopting measures to benefit businessmen and large entrepreneurs, has failed, and his government has failed, to also single out middle class citizens who are paying a great deal of tax and who are in business in a small way for some tangible economic benefits. For example, even a small reduction in the level of personal income tax would mean that he, and millions like him, would be able to consume more of the goods and services generated by the entrepreneurs. In turn, these entrepreneurs would hopefully increase their production and make available types of consumer goods and services that would herald the economic expansion that we so desperately need in this country to provide, not only a continuing rise in the standard of living, but desperately needed employment opportunities. Members on both sides of this House agree that we must have increased opportunities for employment.
In this particular budget the government has attempted to expedite production ends by giving the private sector the means to expand and increase production, increase its investment, but what about the purchasing means to justify these production ends? Instead of stimulating the general purchasing power of middle income Canadians, in effect this government has taken away the 3 per cent advantage these people had, so the effective tax rate has been increased rather than decreased. This was a regressive step for which this government will have to answer.
If "faith without works is useless", according to the Biblical adage, then surely economic growth and production capacity increases without the means to consume is also useless. Something should be done, in my opinion, to change at least the attitude, if not the policy, of our Canadian banks. They do not have the proper philosophy in financing Canadian enterprises. These banks, for example, have received concessions from various governments over the years. At the present time, according to the report of the Auditor General, $100 million has been made available to them, without cost supposedly, as compensation for cashing various types of government cheques. As I understand it, by law they are obligated to cash these cheques anyway. Canadian banks in my opinion, are too reluctant to take risks. Perhaps an amendment to the Bank Act to actively encourage our chartered banks to not only finance projects, but to actually become involved in them if they are truly Canadian owned and meet certain criteria, would be a constructive step.
If banks were able to, in effect, be participants to some extent in worthy projects, then their assistance and expertise would be available in certain areas of economic development and the banks would be provided with additional and diversified sources of income, which perhaps would ultimately allow them to lend money at lower rates of interest. It is no secret, Mr. Speaker, that some large corporations are now, in effect, in the banking business. They have come into the field of finance with the aid of their retained earnings and large profits. Why would banks not participate, in a converse manner, in the benefits to be obtained from the profits of corporations which they were instrumental in helping to finance or reorganize? I submit it is a concept worthy of study.
Another point I should like to make with reference to financial institutions, Mr. Speaker, is that some particular
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
lending companies and institutions are charging rates of interest which effectively bar needy small businesses from obtaining the type of credit which, in effect, these institutions are urging them to take. It seems to me, for example, that the Industrial Development Bank is a prime example of an institution which sends some of its personnel about the country encouraging and advising small entrepreneurs to take advantage of their expertise and available moneys, but they miss the point that people cannot afford to pay the kind of interest rates that the IDB charges. They cannot afford, either, the other complications that must result if the IDB takes care of financing, such as incorporation, and auditing procedures which in some cases are not necessary. Perhaps I will say more about this a little later, with reference to some of the problems that are facing some of my constituents.
I should like to touch briefly upon another topic which interests me in the provisions of the current budget. I am speaking particularly about the provision dealing with moneys held in trust for disadvantaged persons. This particular provision is found on page 16 of the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance on May 8. In essence, as I understand it, a person who is crippled, or to use the example given by the hon. minister, a victim of thalidomide poisoning, will not be taxed on funds held in trust for his or her benefit until they reach the age of 21 years. To me, this is a rather ridiculous situation. While conceding that it is a good measure and commending the Minister of Finance for introducing it, it seems to me that its effect, or its thrust if you will, is spoiled by putting in an age limit. If a person is under a disability which can be cured through the passage of time, or there is a change in his or her status, fine; let the tax advantage also be removed. But to put a limit of 21 years of age for tax purposes on moneys held in trust for crippled or disadvantaged persons is very ironic. Age has nothing to do with it, and the person's situation or status, or economic circumstances, are not liable to change through the passage of time. Such a person will not become more capable with age, for example, nor will his disability lessen, at least not in a case such as a thalidomide child. Why have this distinction in there? It spoils the entire effect of an otherwise humane provision.
Another implication of the budget which interests me greatly is the apparent lack of federal-provincial co-operation and consultation. For example, although the federal government has manifested clearly its intention to stimulate private enterprise by lowering corporate tax rates, some of the thrust of its policy may well be lost because the government has not had the consent or the co-operation, at least apparently, of some of our provinces. I have the impression that the provinces of British Columbia and Quebec, for example, will not necessarily change their logging tax provisions in order to expedite the federal government's policy with regard to pulp and paper producers. It seems that the tax rate paid by these companies will be higher than that the Minister of Finance intended, since the provinces will not, I think, without some negotiation change their logging tax provisions.
I have heard much, since becoming a member of this House, of federal-provincial co-operation. Conferences

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
have been held between first ministers and ministers of various departments, federal and provincial; however, as yet, from my position in this House, I have not seen much tangible evidence of federal-provincial co-operation either in the fields of finance or the environment, or, for that matter, in the field of social welfare, as the present situation in some provinces seems to indicate. I think this budget also illustrates that there is a great need for continuing efforts by this government for consultation with the provinces, particularly in the fields of taxation. There is much controversy in the maritime provinces and across the country about provincial governments moving into fields vacated by the federal Minister of Finance. Enough has been said about this already. The point has been made.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, if I may to avail myself of an opportunity to speak, as is traditional in debates such as this, about some of the needs of my constituency. I will do so briefly. I should like to begin by asking the rhetorical but also pointed question, what do our people do when they can no longer follow their normal way of life? What do fishermen do when they are paid for their equipment but told they can no longer fish? What are our miners to do when they are forced to cease a way of life they have known, in many cases, since first entering our work force? Farmers as well face similar difficulties when they find they can no longer make a living in their traditional way. It is all very well to compensate them according to some fixed and, according to definition, equitable scale. All the same, what are they to do? Where are they to go once their means of making a living has been taken from them?
The needs of Nova Scotians in general, and the people of Central Nova, in particular are well known and well defined. Our province needs development, not only by large corporations and government agencies but, as well, by the initiative of its own people, particularly in small ventures which are suited to each region. Hard times in the maritime provinces during this government's tenure of office have become proverbial. Unrealistic transport rates have been set and often discussed in this House. I am pleased that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) alluded to this aspect in his speech which I have had the honour to follow. It seems to me, in view of what the minister said, that it would be appropriate if I were to introduce a few statistics, as it were, to illustrate our difficulties with transportation. For example, after talking with a friend, Mr. C. P. MacLean of J. W. Macdonald Co. Ltd., who operates a business in Central Nova, I learned that in 1966 it cost the company $1.83 per ton to ship scrap iron from New Glasgow to Sydney, Nova Scotia. In 1968, the rate went up to $2.45 a ton. This year, it costs $3.49 a ton to ship that amount. The greater amount paid in many cases means that there is to be a loss instead of profit. I also learned that, to ship steel to Newfoundland from New Glasgow, N.S. via CNR, costs $20 per ton whereas it is possible to ship steel from Detroit to Newfoundland for $6 a ton. This will show what businessmen in the Maritimes are up against.
In my constituency, we honestly applaud the efforts of the government to develop and open our north. We support that as a national goal, yet we are apprehensive to some extent about the ecological implications and rights

of the native peoples involved. We wonder, too, at the spending of all those millions of dollars for highways to the north-Perhaps not all the implications have been thought out-and yet not even $1 million or $2 million have been allocated to construct a highway to open an area in my constituency in Guysborough county, where the need for such a highway is so obvious that for years reference has been made to the "missing link highway" between the areas of Port Bickerton (Fisherman Harbour) and Country Harbour. This is a development so necessary that it is difficult to see why it has not been expedited before. Mr. Speaker, the whole of the eastern shore of Nova Scotia has been neglected.
The Industrial Development Bank, if I may return to that subject, is not the answer to the financing of a small business. There is too much red tape; there are too many conditions and too high an interest rate is charged for that purpose. What we really require is an agency like an ordinary mortgage corporation which would be given incentives to finance small businesses or even to finance the construction of homes outside well defined town boundaries. In that way, aid could be given to the development of the rural parts of my constituency and province and, to some small extent, help halt the rush towards centralization in urban areas. We may be comforted by knowing that this administration is at least considering taking steps in this direction under its residential mortgage financing legislation. Its scope ought to be broadened and it should be extended to cover the building of small commercial buildings in the eastern shore area of my constituency. The same thing could be said about many other areas where people would like to establish small business enterprises which could be tailored to take advantage of what can be found in those areas.
One sees examples of this in the New England states. For example, people in the area would like to grow and process cranberries, foxberries or blueberries, not only for the tourist trade, but to ship to canneries and food processing plants; they would like to sell scallops and fresh sea foods at roadside booths; to serve good clam chowder and home cooking, to undertake small boat building operations or conduct salt water sport fishing tours; to experiment with aquaculture for clams or oysters; and, to provide necessities such as trailer parks and other amenities for tourists. But, Mr. Speaker, they lack capital. Capital is very necessary, and this budget makes inadequate provision for the kind of capital which is needed if we are to help these areas in Nova Scotia.
This particular budget, as I have said before, is fine for healthy, large corporations which need assistance to improve their competitive positions in major markets, but it does nothing to encourage Canadians who wish to start in a small way and become independent. It does not help the average person to begin a small business.
This government has done nothing constructive to assist the Sheet Harbour area of Nova Scotia, although the matter has repeatedly been brought to the government's attention in the House of Commons by myself and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). That is to say, nothing has been done to compensate for the loss of the pulp mill, which was the only industry of any consequence in the entire shore region, apart from
June 12, 1972

fishing; and we all know the difficulties in which the fishing industry finds itself because of the extremely timid and reticent attitude, if I may describe it in the kindest terms possible, of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and of the Minister of the Environment and Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis). Surely, Mr. Speaker, the much heralded Department of Regional Economic Expansion could have done something to establish an industry somewhere along this line, in this vast stretch of territory, that would to some extent make up for the loss of the pulp mill which was closed many months ago.
In another area of my constituency, Mr. Speaker, that of Pictou county, there are different problems. It seems obvious that in this area, which is more organized and which has a reasonably diversified industrial type of economy, steps should be taken to have it declared a designated or special growth area within the meaning of the DREE legislation. In this connection, may I quote from part of an article which appeared in the recent Halifax edition of a leading newspaper. It is entitled, "Grits to impose metro government" and, in part, reads as follows:
There are indications that the Nova Scotia government now is prepared to move firmly toward some form of regional government for the Halifax metropolitan area.
In some ways this is comparable to the industrialized area of Pictou county, to which I referred. I continue:
-pressure from the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion (DREE) for some overall planning for this area could force the provincial government to move steadily towards regional government with or without the blessing of the three local municipalities.
I wonder if the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is trying to exert political pressure on municipalities. For example, are municipalities being led to believe that they will not be designated as special growth areas unless provision is made for a certain type of local government? If so, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion should say so, and not beat around the bush on this subject. I appeal to the government directly to do something and take care of the situation in Pictou county. It is an area that is fast growing industrially and needs all the help it can get particularly in view of the government's transport policies.
I, personally, am most concerned about what is happening to agriculture in Nova Scotia, about the steps being taken to alleviate difficulties. I still live in a farming community and have seen the drastic decrease in livestock and farming activity in my area. It might be useful if I were to put on the record at this time statistics to show the drastic decline in farming in Nova Scotia over the years. In 1935, for example, Nova Scotia produced 4,900,000 pounds of creamery butter. At present, Nova Scotia produces less than half this amount. Milk production is down drastically, and there are fewer cattle. The same may be said with regard to sheep. What is really disconcerting is the fact that a census of farms taken in 1931 revealed there were 39,444 farms. Thirty-five years later there were only 9,621, less than one quarter. Consolidation accounts for some decrease in numbers, but consider this, Mr. Speaker. The area of improved land dropped from 2,502,773 acres in 1933 to 1,084,273 acres in 1966. That is a tremendous decline.
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
In Canada as a whole, if my figures are correct, it appears that the census of farms reveals a decline from 430,522 to 366,128. Total farm land in Canada dropped to 169.7 million acres from 174.1 million acres. That is further evidence of the decline in the agriculture industry. If we are to stop this alarming trend and protect a way of life that has been so good to us and for this country, many government ministers and departments will have to help, not just the Minister of Finance. Surely, we do not want large corporations to be completely pre-eminent in agriculture, yet our present tax policies are forcing the small farmer out of business and into cities where, in many cases, he becomes a sort of refugee. When a man sells his farm and moves to the city, often he cannot adjust. A man who owns land has a stake in this country. He can grow crops, raise animals and contribute something. If you take this way of life away from a man who is used to it, he becomes, in some cases, a burden and not an asset to society.
There has been so much abuse heaped on the government regarding its policy on foreign ownership that one almost hates to kick a government when it is down. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recognized the inadequacies of this policy when he asked students in the western part of this nation not to be too hard on it, or words to that effect. This government had a problem regarding the Gray report. It had to take some action, make some gesture before an election. Since the basic contents of the report were leaked, the report could not have been left in limbo indefinitely. Last year the Home Oil takeover bid embarrassed the government. The year before, 1971, Denison Mines had to be dealt with, so the government gave us the Gray report. The basic truth is that it does not have much, Mr. Speaker. Like so much that this government does, it is hardly more than a gesture. If a foreign company wishes to take over a Canadian one but is prevented from doing so, it can start a new company and possibly put an existing one out of business as a result. We must give incentives to Canadians to develop and invest in our own companies by granting tax credits, using a selective capital gains tax or some other device whereby it pays to be a Canadian in Canada.
The former Minister of Finance made a step in that direction when he recognized that small Canadian-owned companies should be treated more equitably with regard to corporation taxes, but more of this spirit is needed. All hon. members must be rather apologetic about this so-called Gray report if this is the best that our government can do. If all we want to do is screen American takeovers, I predict we will see Americans come in and by-pass these provisions by starting their own companies.
We need to limit control in certain key areas. I do not know exactly what Mexico has done over the years, but my information is that the Mexican government has done very well in coming to grips with its foreign ownership problems. In future, if the administration of Mexico wishes to pursue a course of economic union or some scheme of this nature, that is pursue a continentalist policy, they can do so with their national pride and economic strength apparent and intact. A country that is in control of its economy could, when the occasion arises,

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Whiting
participate in a continentalist policy in some areas, but could refuse if it had to participate as a junior partner with a tiny, minority interest. How can one conduct meaningful policies from a posture such as this? I sincerely hope, and I trust my feelings are shared by the administration, that this government can come up with progressive legislation that will give Canadians a positive incentive to develop their own country so that in years to come we will be pre-eminent in our country and not so utterly dependent, as we now are, on foreign capital.
In conclusion, I say to this government that they have only scratched the surface with their foreign ownership policy and budgetary proposals. They are not all bad, but in my humble opinion, they are not all that good. The tax reform legislation is not cohesive and it is not conducive to economic growth. This government has failed to coordinate its efforts with provincial authorities. Instead of talking to the provincial authorities, they have been talking at them. When some of the fellows I worked with in the woods showed up with a fat lip or black eye, I asked them what happened and they replied that they were talking when they should have been listening. This government has been doing too much talking to the provinces and not enough listening. There has not been the degree of co-operation that is necessary between federal and provincial authorities if this nation is to develop properly. The taxation policies have made it very difficult for Canadians to expand their own nation. As the immortal Joe Louis used to say when he was fighting, "they can run, but they can't hide". The Canadian taxpayer can also run and pay, but thanks to the existing tax policy, he has no place to hide any of his assets, not one little area he can call his own when it comes to putting something aside for his old age. I do not think the majority of people in Canada are happy about this policy. Unless this government does something to change it, they will be in for a very rude shock in the not too distant future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on his initial budget which has set priority on the stimulation of Canada's economy. No one can question the need to provide jobs and to aid the competitive setting for secondary manufacturing, particularly in view of the recently announced United States DISC program.
The reduction to 40 per cent in corporation tax is expected to maintain the buoyancy of our economy and, to some extent, compensate for the squeeze on profit margins due to appreciation of the Canadian dollar. It is also expected to help defuse the threat to Canadian production as a result of protectionist moves by our trading partners. The fast write-off of equipment and machinery is expected to maintain the buoyancy of our economy and stimulate further investment within the secondary manufacturing industry. The result of such stimulus on Halton, which houses a bourgeoning secondary manufacturing sector employing more than 16,000 people, can be of immense importance.
[Mr. MacKay.l
J. P. R. Wadsworth, President and Chief Executive, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, struck a responsive cord with this comment on the budget when he said:
It has a refreshing tone and is positive in outlook.
I think this is the way all Canadians should look at the budget. It is not intended to be a cure-all, nor is it an attempt to buy votes. It is a highly pragmatic program for the continued development and expansion of our economy.
One tax expert, William A. MacDonald, in the Financial Post, of May 13 suggested that this budget, and I quote:
-constitutes a change in tax direction that could have greater long-term implications for the well-being of Canadians than the complex tax reform which took 10 years to hatch. It is directed at strengthening the international competitive position of the economy on a long-term basis-something no budget in recent memory showed any concern about.
"For the time being, at least", said MacDonald, "the fine-tuning and fiddling-at-the-edges of recent budgets has been abandoned in exchange for powerful, direct and permanent action through tax cuts and fast write-offs. These will help the cash flows and rates of return of Canadian manufacturing and replace continuing reliance on government expenditure and loan programmes."
It should be noted, I might point out, that the budget is also in keeping with the approach to foreign investment reflected in the bill introduced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) to provide for the review and assessment of takeovers of Canadian business enterprises by non-residents. The old adage "let the dice fall as they may" can no longer be equated to today's global community. The initiative for throwing the dice lies with the player, and the social consequences of the throw must be shared. So must it be with today's international economy.
The governor of the Bank of Canada put it quite succinctly when he stated:
Because prosperity and depression can spread rapidly from one country to another, the great countries must manage their affairs well and keep firmly in mind the international implications of their actions.
For Canada, it is imperative that government, industry and each individual share equal responsibility in making this nation competitive and stronger.
Focusing, now, on my own constituency of Halton, one of the major beneficiaries of this budget will be the Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited, which now employs more than 7,000 people. That is a lot of employment centralized in one community industry, and much of the county's prosperity depends on this industry. This dependence comes in the form of supplier-to-manufacturing operations: housing for employees, transportation, and many other relevant services, all contributing to increased employment. I would expect Ford as a beneficiary, to heed the advice given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) at his budget conference: "I expect business to get out and hustle, to grow, to compete and to build jobs for Canadians."
Equally important is the need for government to give Ford the opportunity to compete and provide jobs, emphasizing again the need for shared responsibility. Ford, I am sure, intends to be a viable Canadian enter-
June 12, 1972

prise. Recently the president of that company, in an address at the St. Thomas, Ontario, plant, said:
We intend to meet the import challenge of vehicles made in countries other than the U.S. and we intend to meet it with our own resources. Every import sold in this country jeopardizes Canadian jobs and tax revenue.
In effect, the budget protects a very large and important segment of Canada's manufacturing industry; it protects jobs, and it protects against a loss of corporate tax revenue. Labour is viewing with alarm reports circulating that Canada must capitulate on the auto pact in the forthcoming rounds of trade negotiations. Members of the United Auto Workers told the Canadian Labour Congress when they met in Ottawa a month ago that U.S. economic strategies are costing and will cost the Canadian automotive industry thousands of jobs. Dennis McDermott, Canadian director of the U.A.W. said "The Americans are playing around with the auto pact and we think they're in violation of GATT".
I feel, personally, the reasons we refused to abandon the auto pact safeguards in our talks with the United States in February are valid today and will be applicable tomorrow and years hence if our economy is to progress. However, Ford will only continue to be a viable industry and provide opportunities for spin-off secondary manufacturing operations as long as the auto pact safeguards are maintained in bargaining with our neighbours to the south. The auto pact was a conscious decision by both governments to build a more efficient automotive industry within North America through specialization and rationalization. To this extent, both governments have succeeded.
We have succeeded, I think, because of several very important reasons. First, our labour force is much more skilled and self-disciplined than its counterpart in the United States. Another factor is the excellent social environment in Canada's manufacturing locations, as compared to that of the northern industrial sites in the United States. The Canadian worker can compete, as efficiently and as effectively, as any worker in the world. He is prepared to share responsibility in making our country a better place in which to live, but he must have the co-operation of industry and government. This co-operation is implicit in the auto pact, for, despite all the misconceptions surrounding this agreement, its safeguards stalemate, to a great extent, any moves on the part of the U.S. parent corporations to maintain operations in Canada only as long as it is profitable for them to do so.
In the foregoing remarks, Mr. Speaker, I have touched on those points in the budget which I feel are of vital concern and benefit to the people of my constituency. With the emphasis the minister has placed on the tax benefits for secondary industry, I foresee a marked continuation of the upward trend in employment especially in the auto industry, and I think it is reasonable to expect that all parties involved, both management and labour, will recognize the need for co-operation. As I pointed out in my references to the auto pact, Canadian labour is skilled and self-disciplined, both vital factors in manufacturing efficiency. Given stable labour relations, Canada can maintain its competitive position throughout the world. We also have every right to expect the industry will lower its prices.
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
As the Financial Post stated a few weeks ago:
It is now very much up to business, especially manufacturers to respond to the sizeable tax incentives with substantially more competitive prices.
And now, like the current stories that have the good news and the bad news, I have given you the good news in the budget first. While home in my constituency over the past few weekends I heard what might be called the bad news. Many people mentioned in conversation that the middle income group must continue to carry the chief burden of taxation. Indeed, it is pointed out there is no indication that the 3 per cent reduction introduced in a former budget will be continued after its termination date on December 31 of this year. In other words, we can expect a tax increase of 3 per cent at that time.
I think that all members of the House deplore that the Finance Minister has seen fit not to continue this tax benefit beyond its expiry date. His reasoning is simply that there are many things that we as a country cannot afford today and this is one of them. But I am happy to see that he has not completely closed the door and that he has both the time, between now and the end of the year, as well as the right, to review the legislation so that it will not be necessary to restore the tax at that time. There are other items I might have touched on but they have already been dealt with by previous speakers.
Let us remember, however, that the main thrust of this budget is the creating of jobs and job security while minimizing inflationary tendencies. In my opinion, its short term effect will be to give the economy a definite impetus while laying a solid foundation for future economic growth.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I were to give the members of this House one guess as to the subject about which I intend to speak this afternoon, they would all guess correctly. I rise to speak again on the subject of pensions, because I have learned during the years I have been here that the only way to get action on a matter of this kind is to keep it alive.
I want to say to the Minister of Finance that although it was a bit of a departure from the usual routine that is followed in a budget speech for him to announce certain legislation respecting pension changes, it was a welcome departure. Indeed, the fact that that departure was welcome has been demonstrated by the fact that the two pieces of legislation that he announced on May 8 have already been put through all stages in this House. Thus, the stage is set for the paying of the increases provided in those bills at an early date. I am referring to the increase that will be enjoyed by old age pensioners because the escalation clause has been put back on the basic $80, and also because the 2 per cent ceiling on the escalation provided in the Old Age Security Act has been replaced by a formula that provides for both the basic pension and the guaranteed income supplement to be increased automatically each year in accordance with the actual percentage rise in the cost of living.
The other change that was announced, and which has now been embodied in a statute passed by this House, makes it mandatory for the same principle to apply to

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
pensions paid to war veterans under the Pension Act, to the allowances paid to war veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and to all other pensions and allowances that come under the aegis of the Department of Veterans Affairs. As I say, these announcements which the Minister of Finance made on the night of May 8 were most welcome, and the House has shown that fact by taking speedy action on the two pieces of legislation that were forecast by that announcement.
However, I feel that I must say to the Minister of Finance and to the government that in terms of the total problem, in terms of a really satisfactory pension program for all the people of Canada, all he did by his announcement on May 8, and all the government has done by its subsequent legislation, was to admit that there are things that sorely need to be done. We argued for a long time that it was not good enough to have an escalation clause that was limited by a 2 per cent ceiling. We argued that such a clause had the effect of forcing people to fall behind year after year, especially when their pensions went up by only 2 per cent whereas the cost of living may have gone up 4 or 5 per cent or even more. We are glad that the 2 per cent ceiling has been removed under the Old Age Security Act and that the principle has been established that the escalation of pensions should be related to the actual increase in the cost of living.
The first of four points that I want to make this afternoon, a point I make with as strong a plea as I can, is that this principle of the escalation of pensions according to the actual rise in the cost of living should be extended to every pension plan that comes under the responsibility of the federal government. I know that in response to questions I have asked since May 8, the assurance has been given that these matters are under consideration. But the fact is that we have to be told about 47 times that something is under consideration before we get action.
May I make particular mention of the pensions of retired public servants. For a couple of years now, these people have been getting annual increases in their pensions, but they have been limited to 2 per cent per year. The same is true of retired members of the Canadian Armed Forces and retired Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel. They, too, are getting annual escalations of their pensions but they are limited to 2 per cent. If it is correct and proper, as I assert it is, to put escalation of some pensions, notably old age security and veterans pensions, on a basis that equals the actual increase in the cost of living, I urge that this also must be done for all other pension programs.
I particularly mention retired public servants, retired RCMP personnel, retired members of the Canadian Armed Forces, retired employees of the Bank of Canada, and many other individuals and groups coming under federal responsibility. I might even note that there is a pension arrangement for retired employees of Devco, and if a certain member were in the House this afternoon the mention of that might raise another argument. But I simply make the point that that pension program also has attached to it a 2 per cent ceiling on its escalation provision, and for all I know there are such ceilings in other plans that may not have been drawn to my attention. The Minister of Finance took a good step forward, and showed

himself to be a candidate for something or other in the future, by being progressively minded and introducing the idea that certain pension escalations be related to the actual increase in the cost of living. My very strong plea is that this principle be extended to all pensions that come under federal jurisdiction.
In passing, since I have referred to the pensions of retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and retired personnel of the Canadian Armed Forces, I want again to make the plea that the escalation of their pensions begin at any time after they go on pension. They face a discrimination whereby some public servants at age 55 can get an escalation of their pensions without having to wait till age 60, but in the case of most retired RCMP and Canadian Armed Forces personnel, they have to wait until they are 60 years of age before that escalation begins. That is a slight digression but I felt it should be mentioned along with this first main point that I am trying to make, namely that if this idea that the Minister of Finance brought in on May 8 is a good one-and it is; indeed, it is excellent-it should apply across the board.
I have cited a number of pension programs that come directly under the responsibility of the federal government. There are some I must also mention that one might say come indirectly under the responsibility of the government in Ottawa. I refer in particular to railway pensions. I start with the pensions paid by Canadian National Railways which were escalated on a one-shot basis a little over a year ago, nothing more having been done since that time. In my view, that escalation should be put on an annual basis, a basis that again should correspond to the actual increase in the cost of living and not be tied to a 2 per cent limit.
Of course, in mentioning the Canadian National I must also mention the Canadian Pacific Railway which is lagging behind disgracefully. Every time we pose questions about both these railways to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), he makes the point that he has more influence with one than with the other. Well, I suppose that is true; but I suspect that if the government really wanted to throw its weight around with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway, it could be almost as effective as it is with the Canadian National Railways.
The particular point that I want to make is that both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific are governed by a piece of federal legislation, namely the Pension Benefits Standards Act. This is a federal statute which lays down the conditions registered pension plans must meet in order to qualify for registration, in order to obtain income tax recognition and so on. I submit to the federal government the time has come when it ought to write into the Pension Benefits Standards Act the requirement that all pension plans which come under that act must contain provision for the escalation of those pensions and that that escalation ought to be on a basis equal to the actual rise in the cost of living. We can look at all these matters in a number of ways. If the government ever considers again at this session the bill having to do with the Canadian National financing we will be back to the pension question, and if the government wants to get that bill through the answer is simple. All it needs to do is to tell us it has made an arrangement with Mr. MacMillan, the
June 12, 1972

President of the Canadian National Railways, to improve Canadian National pensions along the lines we have suggested.
Mr. Speaker, I have been unhappy since it was first brought in that we have had a 2 per cent ceiling on the annual increase in pensions. I take my hat off to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). He has broken through that ceiling, but only in respect of old age security and the pensions of veterans. I call upon him to use his influence with the government to recommend that it finish the job and break that ceiling right across the board, if that is not a mixed metaphor.
I said that I had four things to say. I shall move immediately to the second point. I agree that I am asking for something that will not happen overnight and something which calls for study. However, we must get this study started. A few years ago we did not even have a universal pension and until a short few years ago we did not have any escalation. We have made progress. But I want to say again this is not good enough. It is really not the mark of a decent society if all we can do for our retired people is to increase their pensions in accordance with the rise in the cost of living. Surely our older and retired people who helped make the economy what it is at any given time have the right to share in the rising standard of living. Wage rates go up faster than the cost of living goes up. The gross national product goes up faster than the cost of living goes up. When you give to retired people only an increase related to the cost of living increase you condemn them to remain at the same standard of living they had at the time of their retirement, even though people all around them enjoy an increase in their standard of living.
An editorial appeared in the Vancouver Province on this subject on May 20, 1972, entitled "Standard of living pensions . . .". I admit it was a speech or two of mine which prompted the writing of this editorial. It says some very nice things about me, but I do not know of anything in the rules which would prevent me referring to it because of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You must have a good researcher. I have one or two.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have friends in British Columbia who send these clippings to me. Indeed, I have a great many friends in British Columbia. The article reads:
Mr. Stanley Knowles makes a persuasive point when he says the old age pension should be related not only to cost of living but also to standards of living.
The two measurements are related but they are not the same.
If pensions are increased by a cost of living formula as Ottawa now proposes, they merely keep pace with increased costs. If they are increased by a standard of living formula they allow the pensioner to keep pace with the general improvements in lifestyle that other sections of society enjoy through real economic growth.
The next two or three paragraphs of the editorial are direct quotations from speeches of mine, so I shall skip them and go to the last paragraph:
But if it's considered fair that other people should share in the increased wealth of the country beyond the mere increase in the cost of living, it's equally fair that pensioners should benefit along
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
with them. Such increases would obviously be very expensive. But expense is not a final argument against the principle.
I wish to underline that. The principle is unanswerable and incontrovertible in respect of our older people. I hear they are busy banding themselves together in the United States and calling themselves the Grey Panthers. A program appeared on the CBC last night which members of the government should have watched, or which they should watch some other time if they did not see it, which indicated that the retired people in that country, some 20 million strong, are not satisfied with things as they are. I think the same thing is true here on a lesser scale. I feel strongly that our older people, in numbers approaching 1,700,000 or perhaps two million, are entitled not just to be kept alive on some subsistence allowance and are entitled not just to an increase in their pension year after year to keep them at the standard of living they had at the time of retirement, but are entitled to share in the growing wealth and the rising standard of living in this country. I call upon the government to give some real study to this matter. I think this ought to be brought into effect right away. I know that first of all we must have the cost of living increase applied to every one. I feel, however, that the day should not be far off when we start to put into effect the principle of escalating all pensions according to the rise in the standard of living and in so doing recognizing the rights of our older and retired people.
The third thing I wish to say this afternoon is that after or perhaps even before we have solved these problems about the escalation of pensions of various kinds, a good hard look must be taken at the basic rates. It is fine to say that the old age security pension will now be escalated by an amount equal to the actual percentage rise in the cost of living, but $80 as a basic rate is not a sufficient amount with which to start. It is no answer to say there is a guaranteed income supplement which one can obtain if one subjects himself to a certain income test. I believe that at the present time that basic rate should be not less than $150 a month. I think, too, the basic rate of pensions paid to our blind and disabled people should be increased substantially. I believe it is unfortunate that in the changes which have taken place in our pension legislation in the past few years the rate for blind and disabled persons has not been increased, as it should have been. A pension of $75 a month is not very much; it certainly is not enough. I know these people receive more money than that because they can obtain assistance from the provinces, funded in part out of the Canada Assistance Plan. But I still think that persons who are blind or disabled ought not to have to go through that kind of routine. I believe their right to an adequate pension because of their condition ought to be recognized under federal legislation.
I feel, too, that the basic rates of both pensions and allowances paid to our veterans must be increased. I am delighted that the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing) has indicated his willingness that this question be referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. When this reference is made the House can be sure the committee will study this matter very sympathetically. I want to emphasize that in asking for a new look at the rates with regard to veterans, I have in mind not only the basic rates of the disability pensions paid under the Pension Act, but also the rates of the war veterans allowance.
3050

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. S. Knowles
Those rates must also be increased, and increased substantially.
These matters I bring before the House under the general point that I am making that while I am pleased that we have made progress in terms of escalating pensions, and while I welcome the attention that has been paid to my plea that the escalation of pensions be related to the standard of living, these things are without any significant value unless the basic rates are adequate. It is not good enough in this day and age to have a basic rate of old age security that is only $80 a month, and I regard the basic rate of the disability pension for veterans as being too low in relation to today's standards. In my view, these rates simply must be increased.
I know of course that in relation to this, as in relation to all the requests that some of us make for pension increases, someone may put the question "where is the money to come from?" I do not press what I am now going to say too hard because I know what you can do with bookkeeping, but just in terms of bookkeeping I would point out that the old age security fund is running a healthy surplus, as are all our pension funds, and that the new fund that was established a year or so ago to provide escalation payments to retired civil servants, retired RCMP and retired armed forces personnel is running a healthy surplus. If you want to do it in terms of bookkeeping, there are many items of money of that sort that can be found. As I say, I do not press that too hard because in my view the basic question is what society wants to do and how we plan the distribution of what we produce. I know that there is only so much we can produce, and it is also a fact that in today's thinking in terms of saving our environment, saving our world from destruction by pollution and saving society, we may have to curtail this onward march in the production of more and more wealth. But the real problem is how we share such wealth as we are able to produce, and I am not satisfied that the dividing of the pie as we do it today is good enough so far as our pensioners, our veterans and all our older and retired people are concerned. So I call for a new look at the basic rates of all our pensions and for increases of substantial amounts in those rates.
I said I had four things I wanted to bring before the House this afternoon. Not one of them is new, but they are all put forward in the belief born of experience that it is not what you asked for six months ago or last year that carries any weight; you have to keep these issues alive all the time. The fourth of the issues that I want to press and keep alive this afternoon is that the time has come to lower the pensionable age, at least on a voluntary basis. I do not think there should be any delay at all on the part of the government in bringing in legislation to amend both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to make it possible for those who wish to leave the labour market to draw both of those pensions, certainly as early as at the age of 60. I think also that this is a way in which some solution can be found to the problem of the younger wife who has not yet reached the pensionable age when the husband has. If you had that five year voluntary period, it would solve a great many of these cases.

A moment ago I had the immodesty-not unique among politicians-of referring to an editorial in a west coast newspaper that supported my position on standard of living pensions. I wonder if I may now pick up an editorial from an east coast newspaper, namely, the Halifax Mail-Star of Wednesday, April 19, 1972 which carries the interesting heading "Ahead of his time". It starts off by saying:
