It is not at all surprising to find that the latest move in the House of Commons to urge the government into the payment of higher pensions at lower qualifying ages is being led by Stanley Knowles.
Then, there are a couple of paragraphs that are even more laudatory of my efforts over the years, and the editorial ends with this paragraph:
Someday-and we hope it will be in Mr. Knowles' time-
I can tell the Halifax Mail-Star that it will be-
-there will be more generous basic pensions and, possibly, eligibility at age 60 as he proposes. But the timing will depend upon the nation's ability to pay the bill and the politicians' ability to gear their thinking so as to catch up to the veteran pacesetter from the west.
Who would deny himself the opportunity to put that last sentence on the record, but I do so not just to put it there but to enforce my earnest plea to the members of this House that in their thinking they catch up with the needs of our day so far as pensions are concerned. One of the pressing needs, particularly with the vast amount of unemployment among younger people, is for a provision for retirement at an early age. The time for this change is now. Not many years ago we suggested pensions at 65 instead of 70, only to be told that this was impossible. However, eventually even a Liberal government was able to bring in a bill to bring the retirement age down one year at a time, 70 to 69, to 68, to 67, to 66 and to 65. Why should we not have a bill this year, patterned in the same way if you will, to start lowering the pensionable age under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to 64 years in 1972, to 63 the year after, and so on until we get it down to the age of 60 four or five years from now. I submit that this is in line with the needs of our time and it is very much in line with a rational and sensible approach to pensions. I hope that the House and the government will give it earnest consideration.
I close by simply enumerating the four points that I have tried to make. First of all, I think that the idea of a cost of living escalation geared to the actual rise in the cost of living should be extended to all pensions which come under the direct or indirect control of the federal government. Second, I think the government should now initiate a very serious study of the principle of gearing pension increases to the rise in the standard of living. Third, I urge that the basic rate of all our pensions be reconsidered and that there be substantial increases in the light of the needs of today. Finally, I urge that an immediate start be made on lowering the pensionable age at least down to age 60.
These four changes would make tremendous improvements. I could make a speech in another vein. I could tell of the progress we have made over the last 30 or 40 years, and it has been good. Certainly, we have made real gains in the whole pension field. But in terms of what we can do now, in terms of what our people need and deserve, we
June 12, 1972

have a long way to go. Let us get started now, at least on these four points.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the budget debate. The budget was presented to the House of Commons on Monday, May 8, and the fact that we are only now debating its proposals is indicative of the lack of direction and the indecision of the present government. I welcome the opportunity to speak on this measure, since June 10 was an anniversary for me as I have been some 15 years in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take a good look at the place, Lloyd.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are just getting started.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During these years, I have seen many budgets come and go, but few of them with more promises and less performance than the one we have presently under debate. When presenting this lengthy document, the Minister of Finance at least gave an indication that he understood some of the problems when he said, as recorded on page 1 of his text:
No economy is working as well as it should, if there are men and women seeking work who cannot find it.
That one statement represents the most serious charge that can be laid against the Trudeau administration, namely its waste of our greatest resource, our human resource, and the agony, frustration and humiliation which have been the lot of our unemployed people.
Apparently, the Minister of Finance at least recognizes that 6.8 per cent of our working force is unemployed and, to use his words, need "real jobs, not temporary jobs- jobs that last and satisfy." Some 592,000 people were reported as unemployed in April, and Trudeau unemployment is becoming a Canadian trademark like maple syrup, but it is certainly not as sweet to those who are affected.
Obviously, the Minister of Finance got the message, for right now some 43 per cent of the unemployed are young people between the ages of 14 and 24 years. Unemployment is a disaster for men and women of any age, but young people are especially vulnerable to the loss of dignity, and the hampering of legitimate ambition which is the inevitable result of being unable to find a job.
Further on in his speech, the minister stated:
I believe that part of my responsibility in this portfolio is to take a hard look at the rough edges of tax reform and I intend to see to it that the rough edges are smoothed out.
I ask the minister: where was he when this so-called tax reform was rammed through the House by the use of closure? Where was he when these rough edges were being put on this legislation by his own government? In his budget speech, the minister continued:
I propose to announce a number of important amendments to the Income Tax Act arising out of tax reform. The particular amendments have been selected either because they affect large numbers
The Budget-Mr. Crouse
of taxpayers-or because the government is already committed to make them.
Then, the minister makes an astounding statement. He says:
There are a few other amendments which I have been contemplating-but I have not included these in this budget because I am still considering the best solution to the particular problems. I mention this because many people have made sensible suggestions to me, but it is not possible to deal with all of them tonight.
Talk about Nero fiddling while Rome burns! Is the Minister of Finance not yet aware that it is tax reform legislation which has created chaos, indecision and uncertainty throughout the business community, and that he should have acted in this budget on the sensible suggestions made by many people to him and to his government?
It is possible that the government could have avoided the rough edges of tax reform, injustices in law of which the minister speaks, if it had listened to the sensible advice of the official opposition last year, and delayed the tax bill until its anomalies had been straightened out. However, that course of action did not suit the government which was obsessed with the idea of using its majority power to force the tax bill through Parliament. The present Minister of Finance, who was then the Minister of Justice in the Trudeau government, must accept his share of responsibility for the present numbers of unemployed, for the costly blunders brought about by haste and political tinkering, because he meekly accepted, followed and endorsed the Trudeau policies which helped make these problems a reality.
On page 23 of his text, the minister is recorded as, frankly admitting that things have gone wrong under the Trudeau government, the government he supports. I say this because in his assessment of the budget he states:
I wish I could do everything at once. I am sure that each member of this House, were he standing in my place, would have a long list of priorities of things he would want to change, of inequities he would want to cure. The bare fact of the matter is that we cannot do everything at once. We simply don't have the resources. There are limits to the scope of fiscal policy. There are limits to stimulus and re-adjustment.
This is nothing more than an admission of defeat, a negative attitude which says to the unemployed and to our young people, "Have pity on us because we really don't know how to run this resource rich, well-blessed country, effectively." This is, in effect, what the minister is saying, for there is an old cliche which says that you cannot have your cake and eat it too. You cannot waste your tax dollars and still have worthwhile programs for the sound economic development of the country.
When the minister says, "We cannot do everything at once" what he really means is that the government cannot finance all of its pet projects and still assist industry in the creation of much needed jobs. You cannot build $25 million National Defence buildings and $30 million External Affairs headquarters and still have money to assist industry. You cannot build monuments to the ministers in this capital city, and still have funds to assist industry. It is a hollow sham for the government to say we do not have the resources to encourage employment opportunities for our people. According to the booklet put out by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), entitled "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent"-

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Crouse

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell us about the Tories in Manitoba and Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member who, as usual, is interrupting while remaining in his seat, will have time to make his own speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have already done so. I ask what about the Tories in Manitoba and Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member would listen he would learn something. Incidentally, this booklet cost the taxpayers $72,625, and according to it the government spent a total of $10,767,000,000 in the year 1968-69 to serve 20 million people. According to this booklet the government proposes to spend $15,749,000,000 in the year 1972-73 to serve some 21,600,000 people. And since this book was printed, Mr. Speaker, supplementary estimates have brought this planned expenditure up to $16,012,000,000.
Our taxes have been escalating at a phenomenal rate. It is not honest, fair or just to say that we do not have the resources in Canada to provide jobs. The truth is that the government has been wasteful of our resources, and the wrong policies have been given priority. I cannot help but pity the Minister of Finance who showed such a strong desire to become the leader of his party, with a chance at the prime ministerial post, that he clung to his delegates votes until the bitter end at the last Liberal leadership contest. He was really the "Canadian Muskie" of that day. Now that he holds the post of Finance Minister, he will never get a chance to become Prime Minister. I say this after looking at history, where I find that since Confederation only two finance ministers have made it to the top, and none of them were Grits.
The two were Sir Charles Tupper, who became the sixth prime minister in 1896 after serving as finance minister under Sir John A. Macdonald, and R. B. Bennett who served as finance minister during the Meighen Conservative administration, and who defeated the Liberals under Mackenzie King in 1930 to become prime minister. But it looks as though one part of the history to which I refer will repeat itself for I believe Canadians are again preparing to elect a Progressive Conservative Nova Scotian as prime minister of Canada.
It is obvious, however, that the Minister of Finance recognizes a sound taxation policy when he hears one, or otherwise he would not have used the now familiar Grit tactic of strongly opposing, in Truro, Nova Scotia, on June 7, my leader's proposals as outlined when he spoke in the budget debate, covering a simple method of annually adjusting personal income tax exemptions and rate schedules to reflect increases in the cost of living. The Leader of the Opposition has stated that when he becomes Prime Minister, and that will not be very long in coming, he will implement the constant dollar approach to personal income tax payments, based upon the schedule of tax rates and personal exemptions that were set by Parliament in 1971. The aim of his proposal is to enable Canadians to maintain the 1971 equity in the years ahead. As Progressive Conservatives, we believe that the federal government should rid itself of the vested interest in inflation which arises from automatically reaping enormous
additional revenues from personal income taxes when inflation is running high.
Mr. Speaker, there is a squeaky door over in that corner and I would ask you to close it, shut it up.
We also believe that low and middle income Canadians should not automatically pay a larger share of their real income in federal income taxes, especially if they do no better than keep even with increases in the cost of living. When implemented, the Leader of the Opposition's proposal would restore full fundamental parliamentary control over the effective rates of personal income taxation, which is something that is absolutely necessary but which has been lost under the present ineffective, abortive, rubber-stamping committee system. This proposal when implemented will not stop future tax increases but it will place the government under heavy pressure to carefully scrutinize its planned expenditures and to economize wherever possible before taking its case to Parliament. That is the crux of the matter, Mr. Speaker, and that is what we aim to do.
In my opinion, the Minister of Finance's speech in Truro is significant in that there is not one word in it that refutes, denies, challenges or disproves any of the basic points I have just mentioned. This is understandable, for if the Minister of Finance believes in the basic equity and fairness of the schedule of tax rates and personal exemptions which his party proposed and established in 1971, then he cannot, in all fairness, deny the need for maintaining that equity in the years ahead. The Minister of Finance was really grasping at straws when he suggested our proposal would increase government costs and likely intensify inflationary pressures. In actual fact, the constant dollar proposal could well have a beneficial antiinflationary effect. All we need to do is look at the demands made by the workers who are going out on strike-in this year of the strike-across the nation, and we then realize that much of the pressure for higher wage settlements stems from the workers' realization that under the present tax system they need more than basic increments geared to the cost of living increases just to keep even. At the very least, some of that pressure could be eased through the implementation of the proposal put forth by the Leader of the Opposition. Obviously, the present Minister of Finance, like his predecessor, is long on rhetoric and short on understanding, and these are symptons that are easily recognized by an enlightened electorate. I believe it was Bismarck who said "Nothing can be regarded as true until it has been officially denied by the government." The Minister of Finance's condemnation of my leader's proposals is a strong indication that they have some merit and are worthy of serious consideration by Canadians.
It is obvious to most Canadians that we are heading on a collision course between government and industry under the present government's policies. Nowhere is this more evident than in the field of transportation. Whether you are in western Canada or the Atlantic provinces, the questions raised are all the same. How much longer can this federal government, its Canadian Transport Commission and the railways, ignore the appeals of Canadians for a better break on freight rate charges. When I am in my

June 12, 1972

constituency I am asked, how much longer will the present government pretend that there is consistency in its national transportation and economic development policies? On the one hand, this government has set up the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which makes grants toward the alleviation of economic disparity, while on the other hand it permits rising transportation costs to strangle large and small industries in the Atlantic region. Surely the government cannot claim it has not been alerted to this problem. We have held special debates in this House and our members from time to time have moved a special motion to continue those debates, most of which have been ignored or refused by the government. Surely, they cannot claim that they have not been made aware of the adverse effects on regional growth of the eight freight rate increases in a little more than 24 months.
In his speech today, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) outlined a proposal to pay the freight on goods sold to the government. To use his words, I think he said that "Contracts would be accepted f.o.b. the factory;" that is, on any contract awarded to a factory in any part of Canada by the Department of Supply and Services. Mr. Speaker, this is a move in the right direction, but that is all. It is only a small step; it is no real solution and it is not real transportation policy. For example, if a firm in my constituency desired to tender on steel barges to be sold to the government, first it must find out the cost of the steel which has to be purchased in Hamilton, Ontario and transported to Halifax, Lunenburg, Liverpool, or Shelburne, in Nova Scotia. That cost must be added to the cost of production, and this makes that firm in no way competitive with the company located five miles from the steel factory. That is why I say the proposal put forward by the Minister of Supply and Services is a small step, but it is not a real transportation policy for Atlantic Canada.
There is nothing in this budget which indicates that the Minister of Finance is aware of our transportation problems. In fact, transportation is excluded from absolutely any aid in this budget, yet hardly a week passes without some indication that companies operating in Atlantic Canada are in trouble. Only a few years ago a new company, Anil Canada Ltd. started producing wallboard in my constituency at East Chester and from correspondence and discussions I have held with the President of that company, it is evident that freight charges are seriously hampering their operations. This is only one example, and I could cite many more. We have long since passed the day when the federal government showed any real concern for t*ie transportation ills of Atlantic Canada.
Now, we are told that the Canadian railways will file notices of substantial increases in freight rates with the Canadian Transport Commission on June 19. A 10 per cent increase in rate charges on shipments to and from Atlantic Canada will deal a crippling blow to local industry. This is harsh treatment for our people and it is an action that we simply cannot and will not tolerate. We cannot stand idly by and let this government add further burdens to an already over-burdened economy in Atlantic Canada. When the railroads were built, there was a concept that railways from sea to sea were to hold Canada together. This concept has been forgotten by the present government, if it ever knew it, and I believe that a moratorium should be declared on all freight rate
The Budget-Mr. Crouse
increases, until a fair and just transportation policy has been worked out that is acceptable to our people.
When the National Transportation Act was passed in 1967, Section 3 of that act promised that we were going to have, from 1967 onward, an economic, efficient, and adequate transportation system in Canada that would make the best use of the available modes of travel at the least cost. And this was to be achieved in a way to protect the interests of the users, and at the same time maintain the economic well-being and growth of Canada. The best way to do this, it was stated, was to do it by competition. This powerful regulatory commission operates on the theory that all our problems can be regulated. Unfortunately, the side effects of the cure trigger other reactions that more seriously threaten the well-being of the patient than the illness first perceived. The cost of transportation since 1967 has not become cheaper, nor has it become more efficient as a direct result of regulation. In fact, in my opinion, the Canadian Transport Commission has failed. It has let us down badly because its promise of performance has not measured up to our transportation goals.
This government must not only establish a sound national transportation policy but it must also define a sound industrial policy so that Canadian business, large and small, will know where it stands. At the present time, our businessmen are confused, concerned, and lack confidence in their federal government. This accounts for their lack of initiative in attempting further industrial development which will provide worth-while jobs for Canadians. When you are running a business, and I have some experience in this field, you must have a clearcut objective in order to be successful; you must know where you are going. However, it is obvious to Canadian businessmen that the Trudeau government's industrial policy is comparable to pouring water into a sieve; it runs in all directions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And it is not very thick, either.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe a white paper setting out the government's industrial policy would be extremely valuable in giving business and labour an idea where this government is heading. We are reforming our tax laws and our competition and labour laws without any clear idea of what this government or this country is trying to achieve. This is not good enough. The gap between business and government is widening, Mr. Speaker. What is needed today, above everything else, is the restoration of a climate of confidence and trust. We must, somehow, restore to Canadians confidence and trust in their government; and, conversely, there must be confidence and trust by the government in the Canadian people, if we are ever to hope to get the economy moving again and provide jobs for the hundreds of thousands of people who are looking for work. Our export figures for March of this year document all too clearly our world trading position and our inability to compete in world markets. With the exception of the United States, our exports declined. Exports to Britain, Japan, West Germany, Norway, Italy, Australia, Venezuela, Belgium, Luxembourg and India declined by a total of $78.2 million.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Shame.

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Crouse

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Manufacturing, according to my figures, last month employed 17,000 fewer people in this country. Obviously, this is not good enough, and our export problems are now increasing as a result of the increase in Canada's dollar value and a weak, vacillating Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. For example, low cost imports of cotton textiles are destroying our Canadian producers, and it is doubtful whether Cosmos Imperial Mills can survive in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia without a change in government policy. Our stainless steel producers, especially Atlas Steels, are reportedly postponing indefinitely any expansion plans, owing to import competition from Japan, Sweden, Germany, France and Austria. The government apparently takes the view that, apart from using persuasion to bring down commercial interest rates, there is little it can do about the high level of our dollar or to make our companies more competitive. I, personally, cannot accept that view, for it is still not too late to strengthen further the financial position of our Canadian companies by giving them an immediate tax reduction with respect to manufacturing and processing right across the board rather than waiting until January 1, 1973, as the minister proposed in his budget. Only by enabling Canadian corporations to compete in the world as it is will we be able to provide jobs for our people.
The minister may say, no doubt, that his tax proposals should encourage industry. Mr. Speaker, one of the things this country needs is risk capital. It is all very well for the minister to say that personal savings are increasing in Canada; but he ought to realize, and I know he does, that these savings for the most part are all going into the hands of institutions which invest them in limited areas in order to obtain a safe return on the capital entrusted to them. They are not venturesome. They do not take risks. We do not, under this government, encourage the accumulation of private wealth; and, without money in the hands of entrepreneurs, there can be little or no risk taking.
I have said we need a sound industrial policy; this fact became evident even before the Nixon moves last August for it was difficult to find the basis for a strong, underlying growth trend in Canada's economy. Our plight emphasizes in the most striking way the need for an immediate cleanup of the decks on the economic front if there is to be any hope of our getting businessmen down to business. Instead, we have been caught up in a web only faintly related to the real world of decision and international competitition. The Trudeau cabinet has been so busy trying to do the things that it ought not to have done that it has not had time to do those things that it ought to have done. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker.
This budget has unfortunate implications for federal-provincial relations. The buoyancy in federal revenues has been used by the federal government for its own purposes. Approximately $1 billion at its disposal has been used in accordance with its views. It is the federal government's views on social priorities which continue to dominate, and this centralizing trend is not helping the provinces or municipalities which want to make their own decisions but are desperate for the resources needed to meet their current obligations.
My main objections to the present budget cover a number of areas. In my opinion, it makes little sense to

treat different sectors of the economy in such a diverse way. It is also difficult for businessmen to plan ahead when tax rates are changed so frequently, and when selective tax cuts to corporations are unjust and inappropriate. The tax cut for manufacturers and processors is too indefinite. I ask the Minister of Finance to tell us, when he speaks, what specifically the government means when it speaks of a manufacturer, or of a processor. Why introduce a new set of distortions into the functioning of the market system, by substituting the judgments of the Minister of Finance as to what types of tax relief make for the greatest degree of growth for our competitive system? Frankly, I do not trust the minister's judgment in a matter as delicate and sensitive as this.
Why, for example, was equipment used in agriculture, in fishing, in logging, in forestry, in oil or gas wells and in the extraction of mineral resources excluded from the fast write-off incentive proposals? Once again our agricultural industry and fishing industry have been left standing by the boards, as it were, for all the consideration they have been given by this government. It seems to me that these primary industries provide considerable employment opportunities, and therefore should be encouraged. If the government is interested primarily in job creation, and all current economic texts show that the service area overwhelmingly is the biggest source of employment, why was that area excluded from assistance in this budget? Employment in the service and recreational sectors declined by 12,000 last month.
If countering the American Domestic International Sales Corporation program, commonly known as DISC, was the objective, it would have been more appropriate to introduce a similar plan in Canada to encourage exports. Quite frankly, in my opinion, erratic variations in tax rates do little, even if they are favourable or result in lower tax rates. A budget was brought down in June, 1971, and it was followed by the 1971 temporary tax. reduction last October; then, the tax reform legislation was passed last December, which attempted to set out tax schedules for the ensuing three years. Now, we have another, should I say haphazard, change providing for a 9 per cent tax cut for manufacturers and processors. These shifts make it difficult to plan ahead intelligently or to take advantage of rate changes. Therefore, I believe investment plans will be postponed until there is greater assurance about the outlook or greater assurance as to what future tax rates will be.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: People are waiting for a new government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The attitude of businessmen may well be, "Why do it now; let's wait for the next tax concession." And who can blame them for adopting that posture? Large industrial organizations do their financial planning at least three years in advance; therefore, long term plans must be based on something other than the fickle, spur of the moment changes initiated by the Minister of Finance.

speechtext: Order, please. It is my duty pursuant to Standing Order 40 to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding)-National Parks-Lake Louise project-Request for statement on government position following public hearings; the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie)-External Affairs-Offer of good offices by United Nations Secretary General respecting Viet Nam war-Canadian position-Representation to U.S., and the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nys-trom)-Youth-Opportunities for Youth program-Rejected applications-Results of solicitation of companies to provide jobs.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech, delivered in a very elegant, effective fashion, contains so many stimulating and sensible proposals that it has earned for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) superlative praise. That is the way one can describe the widespread approval of the document that spells and easier load for pensioners and the disabled and more jobs for the unemployed. It is a document, sir, which marks a long advance in Canada's economic and social maturity. It spells confidence, which some people in this country had lost. The need of the time is the recovery of confidence, confidence that we can beat the unemployment problem.
The tax benefits to expand manufacturing and industrial development will certainly stimulate the business community to accept the challenge and become more successfully competitive in selling our products abroad. I congratulate the minister for his refreshing faith of which, unfortunately, members of the opposition appear to have so little.
In a recent news release, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce expressed pleasure with regard to the constructive budget presented by the Minister of Finance. I quote:
"The measures outlined to stimulate Canadian manufacturing and processing industries should do much to reduce unemployment and to make our competitive position stronger in domestic and international markets," said Neil V. German, president of the Canadian Chamber.
The Budget-Mr. Badanai
In particular, the overall effects of the tax measures in the budget will help Canadian industry to offset the adverse effects of DISC.
The Chamber was also pleased with the measures proposed in the budget to relieve the financial burden borne by those groups hardest hit by inflation such as pensioners, veterans and students.
A review of the debate on Bill C-201, a measure to provide for control of foreign ownership of Canadian companies, reveals some misunderstandings but some of the speeches were reflections of pure anti-Americanism. Fortunately, the Minister of Finance does not see it that way. The unrealistic dream of members of the committee for an independent Canada of eliminating foreign ownership is running against a contemporary world trend to internationalism and, in any case, their theories are not valid in the world in which we live today any more than when we needed foreign capital to develop our industries and create jobs to meet the needs of an expanding and growing population. Had it not been for American capital, there would not have been an iron ore mine in northwestern Ontario. I am referring to the development of the Steeprock Iron Mines in the town of Atikokan, 130 miles west of my constituency. Atikokan would still be a small hamlet. It was risk capital that insured jobs and prosperity for hundreds of people working in that area.
I wish to quote from an editorial that appeared in a recent edition of the Calgary Albertan:
In the much-discussed subject of foreign ownership of Canadian industry to that of foreign ownership of Canadian land, both crown-owned and public, there are many grey areas. While this, on the surface at least, appears to be a laudable endeavor, the problems which will arise if the policy is adopted, first on a national, and then on a provincial scale, can be enormous.
If the respective governments really intend to go whole hog on the latest bit of Canadian nationalism, two important points will have to be determined to the satisfaction of all. These are what constitutes a "foreigner," and what constitutes a "Canadian citizen."
In Canada, which will soon reach a population of 22 million, or just about one-tenth of the population of the United States, there are millions of British subjects who are not Canadian citizens, if the narrow interpretation of the word is to be employed. In the first row are the English, Scottish, Irish and Welsh.
Then come all the immigrants from the 23 Commonwealth countries, white, black, and various shades of brown.
As Canada is a member of the British Commonwealth, all of these people possess the same legal rights as native-born Canadians, once they have been accepted for domicile and have settled down in this country, and as such they are entitled to all the rights and privileges of native-born Canadians and those who have emigrated from other countries outside of the Commonwealth but who have acquired Canadian citizenship after residing here for the period prescribed by law.
The first thing that has to be determined therefore before governments get too deeply involved in the land ownership problem is-what constitutes a "foreigner," and whether British subjects who do not hold citizenship papers are to be barred from buying crown lands. Does it also mean that no person except those who hold Canadian citizenship papers are to be permitted to homestead on crown lands?
The new restrictive legislation now under review by provincial governments across Canada, is merely another chapter in the "Keep the Americans out" policy so popular nowadays.
However, the majority of the governments affected do not possess the intestinal fortitude to name the country they are legislating against, so the legislation will be such as to confine the sale of crown lands to "Canadian citizens." It would be very injudicious to name the Americans in legislation of this kind when the whole
3056

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Badanai
country is still desperately anxious to enlist the aid of American capital in the continued development of natural resources and industry.
I can understand why British Columbia, with its miles of ocean front, lakes, plus a myriad of islands, is anxious to reduce the volume of the sale of land to the Americans.
I too have toyed with the idea of following the birds to Victoria, or to acquire a small piece of Salt Spring Island, and there to be nuzzled by the balmy Pacific coast breezes. Every time I think of Alberta's seven to eight month winter, I find it difficult to understand why the Americans, or any other group presently being designated as "foreigners," would be interested in trying to buy Alberta land at seriously inflated prices.
Those who did buy land in the early days of the oil invasion at moderate prices, now possess a solid investment, but times are different now in the wake of the urban sprawl and inflated land values.
I thought that the Alberta government displayed great prudence when it did not rush passage of amendments to the Land Act, at the recent session of the legislature. This is a problem which is by no means as simple as it may appear.
Ever since the North West Mounted Police rode west in 1874 to bring law and order to what is now the province of Alberta, Americans have been prominent in development. They brought in the first big cattle herds from Texas in the early 1880's and in the boom years prior to the First World War, they poured across the border in an unending stream, bringing their furniture and livestock with them. Later, they provided most of the capital for the development of Alberta's oil and gas resources, and practically all of the first geologists and drilling crews were either American or American trained.
For this one reason alone, I find it impossible to join in the "Yankee, Go Home" cry presently being chanted by the Johnny-come-lately minority, whose contribution to development still has to be assessed.
The opposition is forever pounding on the gloomy side of the unemployment picture which, of course, everyone admits is not what the government had hoped it would be. On the other hand, the prophets of doom are trying to make it look far worse than it is. For example, when estimating employment statistics for young people in the 14 to 24 age bracket, the difficulty is to arrive at anywhere near the number of unemployed.
Students who register with Canada Manpower and placement officers at the various colleges and university offices, often do not notify the agency when they obtain work. There is no way of checking up on students who go out to find jobs by themselves. Many students who applied for permanent positions have not notified the manpower centres of their decision to return to postgraduate school in the fall. Several thousand students, unsuccessful in their job search, are flying to Europe and elsewhere and therefore cannot be classified as actively seeking employment. Some unemployed students have taken temporary summer work, or obtained "Opportunity for Youth" grants, and cannot be classified as permanently placed, while others wait until summer is over before looking for work.
Many corporations delayed their hiring this spring. They are still going through the process of hiring at the present time. Some universities now operate on a co-operative plan which staggers the graduates' entry into the labour market to other months of the year. The latest unemployment figures for the 14 to 24 age group available are for March and indicate an unemployment rate of 12.6

per cent, or about 273,000. This compares with 12.9 per cent jobless students a year ago. On the whole, bachelor-level graduates in commerce and business administration are finding jobs; in some instances, there are not enough commerce graduates to meet the demand from the accounting profession. Graduates from the professional schools of medicine and dentistry are always in demand, but others, especially those with just a B.A., find it most difficult to obtain jobs.
Then, there is the woman factor. A few years ago married women did not, as a rule, enter the labour market when their husbands were gainfully employed. Now, even though the husband may have a good job, the wife wants a job too, and when unemployed she registers at manpower centres as well, thus compounding the unemployment figures. Lest I be accused of being against a married woman seeking employment, I should hasten to say that she has a right to look for a job, if family conditions will allow. But let us also realize that the jobless figures do not really mean the disastrous conditions that the opposition are trying hard to convey to the people of Canada.
With respect to immigration, I should at once express my satisfaction with the new Minister of Manpower and Immigration's attitude toward applicants for admission to Canada as landed immigrants. I admire his forthright statement aimed at granting a little more flexibility in the area of personal judgment to immigration officers, such as boosting the point ratings, if necessary, given previously to unsuccessful applicants; in other words, using the criteria with flexible judgment and compassion.
With regard to the Sedgwick report of October, 1970, prepared by a Toronto lawyer who has never had the experience of being an immigrant, I suggest that it be shelved for some other era when Canada will have doubled its present population. The minister, very properly, rejected the contention that visitors are abusing the relaxed immigration provisions; and I would recommend increased reliance on the discretionary judgment of overseas' immigration officials, who are, by and large, the best trained and responsible individuals in the public service. I was pleased to take note of a substantial increase in this year's budget for increasing the number of officers, and of expanding facilities in our immigration offices around the world.
I should also add that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should be congratulated on the appointment of the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mack-asey) who, when he was Minister of Labour, showed his capacity for commiseration in the face of injustice and who, in his new responsibilities, meets the problems of his department with dedication and compassion.
Canada, as a nation, will be 105 years old in less than two months from now. But Canada as a place for European settlement dates back to 1534 when Jacques Cartier came to our coast seeking a seaway to the Orient. He found, instead, a country, vast and beautiful, beyond his dreams. After the first settlers came to this land, the French and the English they were followed much later by streams of immigrants from almost every country of Europe bringing to our shores millions of men and women of many other cultures who made their homes here and helped in the development of what is now a great nation.
June 12, 1972

Baron Tweedsmuir, one of the best known Governors-General of Canada, once said when speaking to Ukrainian-Canadians:
I want you to remember your old Ukrainian traditions, your beautiful handicrafts, your folksongs and dances and your folk legends. Your traditions are all valuable contributions toward our Canadian culture which must be a new thing created by the contributions of all the elements that make up the nation.
It is with this thought, Mr. Speaker, that I express the gratitude of countless immigrants who are now enjoying the privilege of being Canadians.
A dedicated group of citizens in the City of Thunder Bay have taken on the task of organizing a campaign for funds to establish an arts centre which would include an auditorium. This city of 107,000 people lacks a suitable theatre complex to accommodate an average audience of 1,500 people. Every year those in charge of the music festival are hard-pressed to find accommodation for the various events. The various arts' societies, such as the Cambrian Players, the Lakehead Symphony Orchestra and others are experiencing difficulty in finding suitable quarters for their performances. The arts centre complex is also needed for teaching all facets of the arts, workshops and convention meetings. The federal government, under the Local Initiatives Program, has made a grant of $18,720 toward hiring a co-ordinator, a secretary, and ten surveyors to evaluate the need of the community cultural program. For this, the city is very grateful. The Mayor has indicated that the corporation will lend active support and financial assistance to the project it is hoped, which, once underway, the federal government will also assist with a grant or a loan so that this worthwhile project may be brought to fruition.
One of the most exciting projects that has ever been voiced by a Prime Minister of Canada, ranking with Sir John A. Macdonald's vision of a transcontinental railway a century ago, is a proposal outlined by the Prime Minister to build a highway to connect existing stretches of roads from the border of Alberta, at the 60th parallel, to the Arctic Ocean, at Tuktoyaktuk, a distance of 1,050 miles. In a letter to the Globe and Mail of May 2,1972, Mr. P. Pepperrall, a professor of history from Willowdale, said in part:
In the decade of the 70's nearly a century ago, a dream of similar magnitude that was to open transcontinental communication and to perpetuate a Canada from sea to sea was also denounced as a "preposterous proposition", and "an act of insane recklessness". After all, Sir John A. Macdonald's proposed Canadian Pacific Railway to remote British Columbia would be a road to nowhere of forbidding length, built with money he didn't have, over an undertermined route, and through terrain as formidable as any in the world.
Yet these very obstacles, which people ignorant of the Canadian identity considered to be insurmountable, were the very elements which have characterized the Canadian existence, made its people unique, and impelled them to meet the challenge that was the CPR. The sense of interminable distance, lonely space, and rugged vastness was as much a distinctive part of the Canadian character and consciousness as the country that had created it. And to have failed in response to this challenge that was Canada would not only have betrayed the natural tendency and
The Budget-Mr. Coates
uniqueness of the Canadian identity, but also have stifled the thrust that was to carry it as a nation intact over the threshold of the twentieth century.
Canadians might do well to remember the heritage of our Canadian identity, and in particular the solitary figure of Sir John A. Macdonald earnestly making his proposal for the CPR. Sir John was the "old chieftain" whose national dream culminated in the Canada of a century ago, but the Prime Minister may well be the "new chieftain", whose vision of the north builds a Canada for the twentieth century.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the previous speaker. It is good indeed to know that there are men like him in the House of Commons who have faced a great many adversities on the road here and who can speak with a great deal of fervour and enthusiasm about the future of Canada. While I certainly cannot develop the same kind of enthusiasm for his leader that he expressed, I must say it is nice to know there are still some members of the Liberal party with that kind of enthusiasm for the leader of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are lots of them, don't worry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Do you want to get into a contest about enthusiasm for leaders?

I do not mind getting into a contest about that at all. We happen to have two of your members over here who started off with you, and there are a couple more who are no longer with you, so I would not suggest that you start to name names, otherwise you would discover that you are in a greater deficit position now than you were when you started out in 1968. There is also a good possibility that you will be a lot worse off before the end of 1972. Certainly, you will be a lot worse off if you have to call an election.
That was not exactly the way I intended to start my speech, Mr. Speaker, but that is how it has turned out and I do not mind at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. May we have order. The hon. member has the floor and his time will be running out. He should be given an opportunity to make his contribution to the budget debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite apparent that hon. gentlemen opposite are pretty touchy when it comes to
3058

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Coates
talking about leaders. One of the things that concerns them is that they do not know whether they are going to have their present leader when they go into an election campaign or a new leader. This is one of the things to which we are looking forward. We would certainly like to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) take his record to the people. If that happens there is no doubt at all that there will be an elimination of the present administration, perhaps even an obliteration. I am glad to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) in his seat today, since I am sure we can count him as one of the casualties when the next election comes.
There are a number of matters that I should like to talk about. One of them has been developing since 1968 and the situation has become increasingly worse since then. I refer to the problem of transportation in the Atlantic provinces. I have spoken on this subject many times in the House of Commons since 1968. In recent days, we had some hopes that the government would announce a policy which would be of some value and assistance to the industrial community of Atlantic Canada, whose problems are gargantuan. We had hoped that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) would bring forward some proposals which would, at least to a degree, have alleviated the desperate situation that is developing in Atlantic Canada. However, rather than offsetting the seven freight rate increases that have been sanctioned since September 1969, on June 19 we must face an eighth application by Canadian National Railways for a freight rate increase.
I should like to put on the record what some of the businessmen in the Atlantic provinces have said recently regarding what those freight rate increases have been doing to them. Almost every area of the business community of Atlantic Canada has commented, and with very few exceptions they all say that the rates will be like a noose around their necks. Both their profits and, in some instances, the extent of their losses in the days ahead are being affected. One of the industries that we hope will continue to operate, and which has made every possible effort to continue to operate, is Cosmos Imperial Mills Limited of Yarmouth. They have increased their staff in order to increase production in the hope they can stay alive. The vice-president, Donald Cain, as reported in the Chronicle-Herald for June 10, says:
-the company's prices are fixed and cannot be raised or lowered. The increased rates will definitely push losses up-
The company had announced a modernization of the plant which will increase staff by nearly 100 persons, in an attempt to pull the operation out of the red.
It will be harder to compete in all their markets, said Mr. Cain. The company moves more than half of all its goods by trucks now but the vice-president figured the disadvantage. An increase in line with the rail rate increases, as has happened in the past.
In other words, when the CNR increases its rates, the trucking companies increase theirs too.
The production manager of another textile industry here, Bonda Textiles Ltd., said he expects increased rates would hurt them because a lot of their sales are in central Canada and are small orders.
Then we have a comment from another industry. Mr. A. M. King, president of Ven Rez Products Ltd., of Shel-

burne, states that the company was forced to quit the Ontario market some years ago because of freight rate changes. There is one example after another of companies which have had their backs driven to the wall because of one freight rate increase after another. I do not believe it is possible for many Atlantic businesses to stand still another freight rate increase on June 19. I think the government should take all these rate increases, examine them in the context of what they do to the Atlantic business community and make a determination concerning how something can be done to assist the industry of the Atlantic provinces to survive the avalanche of escalating freight rate costs which faces them. I cannot stress too strongly how serious is the situation which has been developing in Atlantic Canada since 1969 so far as transportation is concerned, and how necessary it is to secure federal government action at the earliest possible date.
I should like to turn from the subject of transportation to that of Information Canada, because Information Canada is being discussed more and more everywhere in this country. I note that on Friday the Acting Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), expressed deep disappointment at the inability of Information Canada to meet the objectives the government held for it. When Information Canada was established there was a great deal of controversy about it. We were told that the number of public relations officers in government departments was to be substantially reduced because Information Canada would absorb their duties and make them surplus to requirements.
It came as a great disappointment to me to receive today the answer to a question I had placed on the order paper on February 18 concerning Information Canada, because parts of the question dealt specifically with whether Information Canada had done its job in so far as information officers were concerned. In the first part of my question I asked what was the total work force in respect of government information officers prior to the establishment of Information Canada. In the second part of the question I asked what was the work force of all government information officers at that time. In the third part I asked for the total work force of Information Canada. The fourth part of the question dealt with the cost of Information Canada.
I tabulated the returns. With regard to the first part of the question, I was informed that prior to Information Canada being established there were 937 information officers in the public service. In answer to the second part of the question I was informed that there were 1,062 information officers in the various departments of government. That answer is exclusive of Information Canada. In other words, the total number of information officers has increased by approximately 125 since Information Canada was established, while at the same time Information Canada has 354 full-time employees plus 162 employees involved with expositions.
The total salaries and wages involved in respect of the 516 people on the staff of Information Canada is $3,132,000, out of a budget of $8,406,000 in the fiscal year 1971-72. In other words, we now have 125 additional information officers associated with various government departments plus 516 employed by Information Canada. So instead of

having 937 people involved in the dissemination of information today in Canada, we have 1,578. An article from the Globe and Mail states:
The record of the past six months ... leads one to conclude that it is urgent to consider some projects to justify our budget and existence," says the January 24 memo from Robert A. J. Phillips, deputy director of the service.
The memo was addressed to director-general Jean-Louis Gagnon and is highly critical of the service's operation.
"Virtually all new visible projects have been cancelled though our budget continues to rise." Spending estimates before the Commons allocate $18,354,000 to Information Canada up $3,389,000 from the fiscal year ending next March 31.
The public will judge Information Canada by what it does and it is unlikely to justify its existence only by efficiency in operations it took over, for equal efficiency might have been achieved without the costly overhead of a new department."
I should like to know where the efficiency is, in view of the fact that Information Canada employs 516 people and the government departments employ 1,062 people, an increase of 125 over the number employed before Information Canada was conceived. It is no wonder the leader of my party has promised-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A voice from the wilderness! It is no wonder the leader of my party has promised to eliminate whatever one might call this. One could not call it a department of government, because it was not conceived by legislation. I suppose one might call it an abortion. It certainly acts as if it were, most of the time. Whatever it is, my leader has said that he will do away with it and he will certainly save the Canadian taxpayers many dollars when he does.
Information Canada was in fact created by the ruling party having a director appointed by the Trudeau government, responsible solely to the Trudeau government, and to be eliminated or dismissed at the pleasure of the Trudeau government. Yet this is the organization the government, in its magnanimity, has given Canadians to provide objective, unbiased and full information of the goings-on of government.
The conflict of interest is as dangerous as it is evident. No one can be unbiased about his employer when he is as dependent as the Director of Information Canada, even if he is a former chairman of the Quebec Liberal Party committee-which, I might add, issued an official biography at the time of the director's appointment containing no mention of his Liberal party affiliation. It is a known fact around the House of Commons that members like myself are constantly plagued by numerous inquiries from personnel at Information Canada requesting information they in fact are supposed to have on hand.
Almost without exception, when a question of mine is answered in the House, especially one that is made an order for return, I receive a call from someone in Information Canada asking me if they can have a copy of the question. That is an example of their efficiency. One of the things Information Canada was supposed to do-I read here from some of the directives-was strengthen national identity, and this they were supposed to do by
The Budget-Mr. Coates
using the two official languages as equally creative instruments of information. I discovered the opposite to be the effect.
I have before me correspondence which the Amherst chamber of commerce had with the Canadian government travel bureau. The Amherst chamber of commerce wanted some travel information, and this is what they were told by the Canadian government travel bureau:
Unfortunately, the travel information literature you requested in your letter is not, for the moment, available in both languages. We regret, then, to have to inform you that it is impossible for us to provide you with the copies requested.
In other words, if they do not have the information in both languages, it is not available-nobody gets it. It is no wonder the government does not know what to do with Information Canada. It is no wonder the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) says he is disappointed in it, and it is no wonder the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) says that when we become the government he will do away with it.
The preceding speaker spoke about two matters in relation to foreign capital. One was with regard to the establishment of industry in Canada by foreign capital, and the other was with regard to the purchasing of land by foreign residents. I cannot get excited about where the money comes from to establish industry in Canada. I think the important thing, especially when we have an unemployment rate of 10 per cent or more in the Atlantic provinces, is to develop our resources and see that our people have jobs. It is only after they are all working that perhaps we can start becoming selective.
I think it is important that we have the right type of base, that companies which establish in this country become good citizens of our country while they are here. So long as that happens, we should not become too concerned about them. At the same time, I think we have to accept the fact that some types of companies we would just as soon not have in this country, especially when they find difficulty in establishing in their own country. An example of this occurred very recently in Nova Scotia when a great deal of discussion took place at the highest level with the premier of that province regarding the establishment of a nuclear power station there.
It is my information that the people interested in establishing that nuclear power station in Nova Scotia were interested in doing so because they could transport the electricity produced to the northeastern part of the United States. One could immediately ask: Why did that company not locate closer to where the power was required-especially in view of the fact that it was an American consortium that spoke about building the nuclear power station?
I gather that the people in the area where the power is required do not wish to have a nuclear power station in their midst. When that type of thing occurs, I think the Nova Scotia government and the federal government should become very concerned. I think there should be definite laws to the effect that a firm which is endeavouring to locate in Canada, one which is not acceptable in the country of its origin, is not acceptable in this country either.
I do not think the province of Nova Scotia should be offering sites to a company producing power for the

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Coates
northeastern section of the United States when all we will get is pollution effects associated with the power produced. So far as I am concerned, and unless it is shown to be otherwise, that is what I would conclude about this nuclear power station.
There is one other point that I would like to make-the hon. member mentioned it also-referring to non-resident ownership of land. Ontario is a large province with many unused acres of land, and perhaps there is no concern here about United States citizens buying up large tracts of land. On the other hand, perhaps there is concern. There certainly is concern in Nova Scotia, especially about speculators buying up large tracts of our recreational and shoreland and using it for promotional purposes for their own benefit.
I have no objection to anyone, anywhere, having a cottage lot in the province of Nova Scotia and enjoying the qualify of life we have to offer, but I do become concerned when American or any other foreign interest buys up large tracts of our good recreational land, thus preventing our own people enjoying those lands now and in the future. They prevent our people having access to our beaches. I believe that steps must be taken, especially in a small province like Nova Scotia which has a limited amount of recreational property and a limited access to the ocean, to prevent those lands from being bought-up and cordoned-off so that our own people and those who visit our area are prevented from enjoying the benefits of the scenery and the quality of life that we have there.
I believe that in the public interest, in places such as Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and certainly in a place like Newfoundland and Labrador, governments must act to ensure that limited amounts of recreational property there are available to everyone. A controversy has been going on in Nova Scotia, and certainly in British Columbia, and action has been taken by some governments in this respect. I am awaiting reasonable action to be taken in Nova Scotia, but not action that will stop anyone from selling property to a bona fide purchaser or, in lieu of a bona fide purchaser, to the government at a reasonable market price.
I think action must be taken along this line to protect the public interest, to protect the people of Nova Scotia and to ensure their right to enjoy what they have in that area of Canada, as well as to ensure that people who visit our province have the right to enjoy it. However, I would certainly not go beyond that and I would certainly not set up any great difficulties for capital coming into this country, because we have many resources which can be developed before we reach our full potential.
I think people who at this stage of our development, with the degree of unemployment we are suffering, suggest stringent requirements for capital coming into the country are fat cats sitting in plush offices who are not worried about where their next pay cheque is coming from. They are not people who are looking for jobs, who do not know if they will have a pay cheque next week. If they were, they would not be as concerned about the establishment of industry by foreign interests as they would be in providing jobs for the people who need jobs-
(Mr. Coates.]
and there are a great many in this country today who do need jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches made in the House this afternoon. I was somewhat surprised by the statements of the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) in as much as almost every criticism he made could easily be refuted simply by referring to the facts.
I know there are some anomalies in the operation of the financial structure of government. I appreciate the points that have been raised by the hon. member who preceded me. However, I think all deliberations within the House of Commons create widespread interest among Canadians but few speeches affect the daily lives of all Canadians. I submit that the budget speech falls into the latter category. In fact, I believe I could get unanimous agreement of the House on that point.
I therefore join thousands of Canadians who have expressed their approval and support of the latest budget, and I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on his well balanced program, properly designed to provide a sound base from which both the public and private sectors of our economy can function and provide more jobs. The minister placed the emphasis of budgetary requirements on the needs of segments of our economic society where it can and will do the most good, not only in the short term but in the long term.
The Liberal party has long stood for social justice on the basis of a gradual but constant program of social reform within the framework of a democratic, private enterprise system, a system which allows maximum freedom to all individuals, including the right to explore their entrepreneurial abilities and a fair reward for initiative. Liberal governments over the years have initiated measures designed to promote greater social justice by relieving financial hardships faced by individuals or groups in our land. These have included, among many others, family allowances, old age pensions, medicare, shared-cost programs with the provinces, unemployment insurance, minimum wages, highway and railroad development, ship-building, the Canada Assistance Plan and scores of programs to alleviate the financial difficulties of farmers, fishermen and the self-employed in all walks of life. The budget of May 8 includes proposals to raise further supplementary pension allowances to enable the pensions of the elderly and veterans to keep pace with the cost of living, to further the tax exemptions for senior citizens, the blind and the disabled and to provide significant tax relief from the heavy burden of education.
It is recognized by all responsible citizens of our country that we do not, and cannot, exist in isolation on the North American continent. While we are, and must remain, alert to the needs of all our citizens we cannot and will not ignore requirements essential to the recognition of the entire economic system, a system which has provided Canadians with the second highest standard of living in the world-and on a per capita basis we enjoy the highest standard of living in the world-a system, Mr. Speaker, that the New Democratic Party apparently seeks to downgrade and destroy in favour of state dictatorship which
June 12, 1972

would rob us of our right to aggressive initiative so vital to all freedom-loving people.
Even though Canada's economy grew more rapidly last year than that of any industrial nation except Japan, prices increased less here than in any other nation. While we can take pride in this accomplishment, I would not suggest-I am practically quoting the Minister of Finance when I say this-that the economy is working at top efficiency while people willing and able to work cannot find jobs.
What about jobs? Where do they surface? The minister has recognized that new jobs can be spawned only by an increase in the need for more workers. He has provided some relief to sectors of the economy which now provide the highest percentage of income to workers. I refer to small businesses, which number in the tens of thousands across Canada, to medium and large corporations and a few giant corporations as well.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock.
At 6 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of calling it six o'clock when I was discussing the importance of employment and jobs and how our government and, I certainly agree, all governments place a special importance on jobs for people. This is really the basis of a democratic society. I asked these questions: What about jobs? Where do they surface?
I would like to ask now: What about jobs? How are jobs financed? Contrary to the preachings of the New Democratic Party, my good friends to the left-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The far left.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-the far left, and some members of other opposition parties as well, jobs do not just happen. Contrary to the preachings of the New Democratic Party and some members of other opposition parties as well, jobs do not just happen: they must be financed by money which is surplus to operating and living costs. It is not possible to provide new jobs without funds made available for expansion of facilities and development of additional markets. Jobs are one of the most important facets of our society. In other words, Mr. Speaker, without risk capital in the hands of those willing to invest in an expanding economy, the rate of decrease in unemployment can be seriously retarded. We have many situations to prove this point. What about jobs? Is profit important or essential?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that "profit"-a word which has not been accepted as well in the last few years as it used to be, but which will surely be accepted again-stands almost alone as a source of risk capital. How much risk
The Budget-Mr. Pringle
capital do we get from our wages which we spend entirely on living expenses and which we need to keep our homes and to provide our families with the necessities of life and the recreational facilities so important to us? How much surplus do we have to provide risk capital? Not very much! It is the philosophy of my friends in the socialist group that business should operate on a break-even basis. That has bankrupted many businesses, Mr. Speaker, and I submit that if we in this country attempted to operate our business on a break-even basis it could bankrupt our workers and our new opportunities almost overnight.
It therefore follows that economic expansion necessary to provide more jobs and increase purchasing power can only be assured by permitting more funds to accumulate as risk capital or profit. The Minister of Finance has recognized this need, and I am convinced that thousands of Canadians will respond by again initiating a new wave of production expansion. In my riding there is already an indication that this is taking place. The minister has proposed reducing the top rate of corporate tax on manufacturing and processing profits to 40 per cent, and the rate on small business to 20 per cent as of January 1, 1973.
I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, the importance of the small business in Canada. When we talk about corporations, it is thought we talk about giant corporations, that we think of those corporations operating at Windsor and areas such as Toronto. Nevertheless, we must think about the thousands of small businessmen who line the main streets of our nation. They are the backbone, the people who provide jobs for other people of their areas. We must think of the small operator, the dairy producer, the man who operates the small store in our small towns. People like that have not disappeared. Some of them stay open after hours, for which they earn extra recompense. They provide a real service and fill a real need of our consumers. It is unfortunate that we seem to refer to giant corporations when we speak in this House of corporations, because the real backbone of this country, in my opinion, is still the small businessman.
The minister has also proposed that we should permit manufacturers and processors to depreciate fully the cost of machinery and equipment acquired, after budget night, within a two-year period. This provision is not being enacted for the giants alone; it is being enacted for the smaller processors of our nation as well as for the manufacturers: it is to benefit those in business in all parts of our country who need to be given an incentive to provide more jobs. To allow them to do this, they will not be so heavily taxed. They now know that they will not need to pay such a high percentage of their profits to the federal government but can divert some of this money and produce jobs with it.
The manufacturing and processing sector, Mr. Speaker, is the largest single source of employment in Canada, providing jobs for more than one-fifth of all working Canadians. The suggestion that employment of new workers will be negated by automation is nonsense. This concept was loudly expounded following the invention of the cotton-gin during the revolution and has yet to be proven valid. Automation has been used to relieve the worker and shorten periods of labour.

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Pringle
I give the labour movement and its leaders full credit for the leadership they have shown over the years. I have always given them full credit. I know that in the past the leaders of the labour movement provided essential leadership for the people they represented and a reasonable balance was struck. I wish I could say the same thing today, but I am afraid I cannot.
It has also been suggested, Mr. Speaker, that tax reductions to individuals would be preferable to reductions in corporation tax, on the basis that consumers would be given greater purchasing power. The weakness of this suggestion can be seen if one compares imports of products into Canada against increasing Canadian production which is necessary to compete with foreign imports. We are all human: we all buy where we can get the best deal, and we do not always buy Canadian-made products if we want to get the best deal possible by virtue of volume production. An increase in volume of production decreases the per unit cost. Therefore, we ought not to increase the sale of imports but, instead, increase the sale of Canadian products and in that way make it possible for costs per unit of Canadian products to be lowered, to improve. We must encourage Canadian production, not imports. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has taken the right stand in this regard.
I ask, what about jobs? Is inflation on a collision course with jobs? At this date control of inflation is virtually, in my opinion, non-existent. The voluntary approach based on gentlemen's agreements cannot work. Over the years, codes of ethics and gentlemen's agreements have been prevalent. In other words, there has been no shortage of gentlemen's agreements-just, possibly, a shortage of gentlemen.
Economists treat inflation control much as we treat the weather-lots of lip service but really no solution. A suggested cure, Mr. Speaker, which seems to be gaining popularity is the concept of price and income controls. I favour another phrase which in my opinion more properly labels the dilemma: cost control, or controls of all costs. I am speaking of all costs, not just prices charged at the grocery store or the excessive demands of organized wage and salaried earners. In this I do not include reasonable demands-I emphasize that reasonable demands I do not include-but excessive demands I do include. I am speaking of all costs.
If each Canadian were assured that cost increases were to be frozen, then the law would apply to everyone in our society, to those in the professions, to landlords, bankers, land speculators-to everyone. It sounds a bit gruesome, does it not? Well, government control of our daily lives is gruesome. However, I can think of nothing more unfair or potentially discriminatory than selective controls. We learned this during the war, although we do not like to admit it now. Let me ask, again, what about jobs, and what about inflation? These two questions, stated together, remind me of a dog chasing its tail. The puzzle is, which of the two is the dog?
One cardinal fact every processor, every manufacturer knows is that any increase in costs without matching productivity results either in price increase or bankruptcy. Therefore, it has been my experience that any increase in cost without matching productivity is inflationary. I

have never seen any statement contradicting this or proving the concept wrong.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, those responsible for causing increased costs do not always pay their fair share of the increase. Two-thirds of Canadians either live on fixed incomes or are self-employed. The real threat of inflation is felt by our senior citizens, farmers, fishermen and the like. Pension adjustments and tax relief to small businesses, as evidenced in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, will help to some extent.
May I reiterate my congratulations to the minister for the relief to be given to these people through income tax measures, as announced in the budget.
