However, I am disappointed that adjustments were not announced which could correct some of the unfair anomalies relating to excise tax and sales tax. For example, tea, coffee and powdered drinks are exempt from federal sales tax. Ice cream cones, popsicles and the like are free of federal sales tax.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am delighted the Minister of Finance is listening and has shown his interest. Soft drinks, Mr. Speaker, are not so exempt, being subject to a 12 per cent tax which, when fairly examined, will be seen as a discriminatory tax. I will not discuss any comparison that is based on essential, nutritional values. Anyone who has experienced, "coffee nerves" as opposed to the "pause that refreshes" will agree that all these beverages are consumed principally because they provide a pleasant break and, as well, provide some psychological relief of tension. I am not in the soft-drink business, Mr. Speaker. We in British Columbia enjoy a beautiful, balmy climate and drink many soft drinks. On occasions when people in the cold climate of the east would probably require tea or coffee, our people prefer soft drinks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am serious about my submission.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't forget a plug for ice cream, Jerry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Montreal is the biggest consumer per capita.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Of course, soft drinks, tea and coffee all provide an excuse for a break from work. The choice of beverage depends to a great extent on the season of the year and the whim of the consumer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It's the real thing!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is interesting to note that even with the discriminatory 12 per cent federal sales tax, the soft-drink industry has responsibly held prices to a much more reasonable level than brewed tea or coffee. If nothing is done, a rise in price is inevitable and the youngsters of Canada will suffer the most.
I am also concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the lack of direct federal support to the handicapped and retarded. It
June 12, 1972

is true that under the Canada Assistance Plan we provide unlimited financial cost-sharing on a 50-50 basis with the provinces. Where provincial governments approach the problem realistically, and some do, we can help. Unfortunately, there are provinces-I fear that my home province of British Columbia is one-which are willing to provide only inadequate minimum financing though the federal government stands willing, ready and able to pay half the cost. A direct approach on our part, or at least the right to share in administration, could raise the necessary assistance to a more acceptable level.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I remind the House that a more equitable approach to imports of agricultural products should be made by this government. Although the dairy and grain industries enjoy the support of tariff commitments, the small fruit and vegetable commodity groups constantly suffer from off-season shipments of vetetables such as lettuce, celery and potatoes.
Strawberry growers are unable to realize any real stability as a result of the threat of imports from low labour cost countries-such as Mexico. An investigation undertaken by the tariff board last October has not yet been reported to the interested people in the Fraser Valley. The strawberry industry is vital to the Fraser Valley. They supply some of the best strawberries on the North American continent. Not only is the quantity and the economy being hurt by this lack of attention, but the quality of strawberries is being affected. I consider this to be a very important matter and I hope the Minister of Finance will take it into consideration.
A great deal has been accomplished through marketing legislation designed to enable producers to improve stability through marketing procedures. I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). The fowl slaughter policy recently announced by him has been unanimously accepted by egg producers. I do not expect all of those within the sound of my voice to understand the facets of this policy and I will not take the time to explain it. It has been accepted by the egg producers, not only because of the financial assistance provided but because it provides for responsible action by producers to plan production more in line with potential markets. The program will have a lasting effect in helping to stabilize the industry.
I am very pleased to support the motion to approve the recently announced budget. It is a good budget. It has been accepted right across this land. The budget was announced in the House on May 8. This is June 12, and we are debating a budget which has already been accepted by the people. Any speeches of a derogatory nature will certainly be lost as far as the people of Canada are concerned. It is a good budget, as will be substantiated over the coming months.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to pass, but I believe the hon. member for Edmonton Center (Mr. Paproski) should speak.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker-
The Budget-Mr. Paproski

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I understand that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) wishes to concede the floor to the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. But I want to be recognized after the hon. member.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose as long as members can get up and speak in the budget debate there is still democracy left in this country. This is one of the few remaining signs of democracy. Parliament has become hobbled by the government in the application of rules designed to frustrate and stymie ordinary MPs. What is the point of sitting in the House if you are compelled to go along in the stream of meaningless government motions and legislation that often has no real purpose but to paper-over the cracks in our society?
The application of rule 43 has become a joke. The opposition was asked to go along in order to expedite the business of the House, and we did so. Day after day we have members rising with serious and urgent matters in the national interest and trying to focus attention through rule 43, and time and again there is lack of consent. How can you bring to the attention of Parliament lapses by the government, when you have to have the consent of government members? Rule 43 has done more than any other procedure to bring this House into disrepute and make Parliament a laughing-stock.
Canadians are scrutinizing this House. They want to know what is going on. There is no way they can find out. They are wondering if the entire proposition is not a waste of time and money. The opposition sits here while the government brings in legislation, generally insufficient, watered-down attempts to get a few headlines. And when we point out the deficiences, we are stymied by the rules. Parliament should be made to operate for the benefit of the people, and not vice versa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are now being asked to deal with a budget. It is perhaps our only chance to say how we feel- probably the last time before the next election. We are asked to say whether we approve of the government's financial policies, and then the budget goes to committee. We are not even able to vote on the details of the budget in this House. My answer to the question whether we approve the policies or not is very simple. The answer is definitely no. How can you approve policies when you cannot find out what they are?
The former minister of finance has gone to the defence portfolio. We hope he will make as good a defence minister as he did a finance minister. If he does, the enemy will have nothing to fear. His policy was to tax and tax, to get all the traffic would bear, as he once put it. Well, they have been following that policy for ten years and I tell them that they are at the end of the line. The traffic will not bear any more. Canadians are fed-up to the teeth with high taxation: they have had it.

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Paproski
When Canadians have to give up from 15 to 20 per cent of their incomes to support waste and government extravagance, it is no wonder they want to call a halt. It is only necessary to look at the latest report of the Auditor General. Never has there been an indictment of a government in office by an officer of Parliament to equal it. The government has broken all the rules of responsible fiscal accounting.
This government has allowed the bureaucrats to take charge of spending enormous amounts of money. There is no one to call a halt, because the government itself is made up of ex-bureaucrats. When you allow the cats into the dairy, who is going to keep them out of the milk pail? That is what is happening today. Ministers and top functionaries are trying to outdo one another in crazy, harebrained schemes to spend and spend. Meanwhile, unemployment increases, taxes go up, waste goes on and the taxpayer becomes more and more fed-up.
Canadians are paying more in taxation than any nation in the western world, and they are getting less for it. The purpose of the policy was to tax in order to cure inflation. Now we have both taxes and inflation! We were to suffer taxes in order to provide jobs. Now we have high taxes and still no jobs. If this is policy, Mr. Speaker, I'll take spinach.
How long does the government think it can lead Canadians around by the nose? Even its own army of highly-paid flacks, its monolithic support from the CBC, its army of tame commentators and columnists, cannot go on convincing Canadians that what they have been subjected to for the past five years is good government. There has never been worse government. Its record is one of confusion wrapped in indecision, compounded by uncertainty.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Beautiful!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where are they going? They are so far behind that they think they are first. They don't even know where they are coming from. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how can they have the nerve to come before Parliament with a document such as the present budget? I am not criticizing the present minister: he inherited the mess. But he is known as the white-haired boy of the cabinet. And now we know how his hair became white. They ended up with a billion dollars more than they had calculated. What fine budgeting that is. It is so scientific. It is certainly budgeting for the scientific age. It is budgeting for the technological age!
Then the government took $750 millions of the billion dollars and handed it to industry. Let me make it plain that I am not objecting to industry getting something. But I do object to this government talking about buying Canada back and then turning around and handing out millions to American subsidiaries as they have in this budget. I think it is high time they took off the mask and stood revealed for what they are-a government subservient to big business and high finance. They know how to look after their own. The Minister of Finance is smiling. I wish they had given a little more to the oil industry and to the construction industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good old Canadian-owned industry!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, no. The industries that get help from the government are those that come around at election time. That is why the government brought down the so-called reform bill to amend the Elections Act in which, once again, the identity of the big givers to the Liberal party continue to be protected. Is that policy? Was it policy to produce a budget in which there is not one red cent for the ordinary taxpayer?
This government has created a financial mess such as we have not seen in this country for many years. And that is not the only area in which they have muddied the waters of public administration. The present immigration policy is inhumane and uncivilized. I refer in particular to the case of Alicia Wiercioch which was brought to the attention of this House by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). Regrettably, he was not given the necessary consent to move his motion. I say "regrettably" because the department showed lack of humanity and bureaucratic heartlessness which was almost unbelievable. It seemed certain that the House would have taken a more humane course. I am sure that if hon. members had known the facts of the case, their reaction would have been different.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister has given the facts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member who interrupted would like to speak, I would be glad to concede the floor. In the application of immigration laws we are dealing with people, people who have suffered a great deal, people who came to Canada to start a new life. They are freedom-loving people. And Alicia Wiercioch was one of these. It is too late now to help her, but perhaps we can at least give her a decent epitaph. She suffered much in Poland. Separated from her husband and with two small children to worry about, she came here from the unhappiness of life behind the iron curtain hoping to find that freedom to which everyone is entitled.
I hear further interruptions. This is the kind of nonsense we have to take over here when we try to call attention to the case of a woman who committed suicide because she could not stay in Canada. It is a stupid system. As I was saying, she arrived in 1968 and four years later her case was still not disposed of. Are people supposed to starve to death in this country? Why are they not allowed to take a job? We give handouts to people who won't work, and we deport people who want to work. There is something seriously wrong about a policy which grinds out and crushes down humanitarian considerations in a manner almost as brutal and ruthless as is found behind the iron curtain. Alicia Wiercioch was driven to desperation and suicide by the inhumanity of immigration policy and the inability of bureaucrats to visualize her problems in human terms.
When bureaucratic regulations are ruthlessly applied without regard for human values, that is not democracy. Members of this House are responsible to a point because we have allowed the bureaucracy to override human rights. We have allowed our powers as legislators to be taken over. We have allowed human rights to be trampled on. How can we tolerate a system through which a mother of two children, whose only crime was love of freedom
June 12, 1972

and a desire to provide for her family, can be sent a bureaucratic ultimatum telling her she is going to lose her chance for freedom? Is this what democracy has come to mean in Canada?
Alicia Wiercioch is not the only victim. I was brought into the case of a Ukrainian girl in Edmonton who would have suffered immediate imprisonment had she been returned to the Soviet Union. And yet this person, because there was no publicity in the case, was told by the department she would have to return. I was able to get hold of the minister who is a very humane man and understands such problems, and a respite was secured. But the minister cannot handle all these cases.
My information is that many people are being sent quietly back to a living death behind the iron curtain. It is not appropriate that a freedom-loving country should be in the position of acting as a kind of enforcer for the iron curtain. This is not what the Canadian people want; at least, Mr. Speaker, not those Canadians who live in my part of the country. Nor was it ever intended that departmental officials should wield the power of life and death over helpless individuals.
The Immigration Department must be shaken up until the officials who are carrying out policies and making these decisions learn the meaning of humanity. The department has to be put under a full-time minister who will see that not only justice but mercy is applied. No one minister can be responsible for dealing with unemployment, manpower direction and training, unemployment insurance and immigration as well. The present minister has too much on his plate. The entire immigration policy must be re-examined because at present its application is inhuman and heartless. Draftdodgers are greeted with open arms while honest, hardworking people whose only desire is freedom are treated like criminals.
The principle must be accepted in law, particularly in immigration law, that people who are patently and obviously political refugees must be given asylum. Freedom cannot be for ourselves alone. Is it the attitude of the government that those who are seeking immigrant status from eastern Europe are second-class applicants? Will anyone say that immigrants from eastern Europe have not contributed to this country?
We are not going to stand still while this government reshapes this country in its own image and likeness. Seven million Canadians who are neither French nor English cannot go on being ignored. Perhaps we should be known as the silent minority. The government is going to hear from the Poles, Ukrainians, Czechs, Italians, Germans, Dutch and other races in this country, including Chinese and Hindus, who are sick and tired of being treated as though they did not exist.
Freedom cannot be a monopoly of the government or the immigration department. People who come here with a desire to be good Canadians and to work for this country should be given a fair hearing. It is time to scrap the heartless and meaningless points system which has no relation to the real contribution and the real value of people. Half of the members in this House could not aualifv under the points system; neither could the majori-
The Budget-Mr. Paproski
ty of officials who are administering it. We do not want any more Alicia Wiercioch cases in this great, freedom-loving country of ours. We do not want people driven to suicide by unfeeling bureaucrats. As far as I am concerned, no single person should be expelled from this country from now on unless and until the case has been brought before the House of Commons, and I ask the government to give that undertaking.
We are elected to represent the people of this nation and to make decisions. I think it is time we took back some of the powers we surrendered to the bureaucrats. I am not asking for explanations from the department because I know what explanations will be forthcoming. I know that this department can produce regulations, memoranda and excuses justifying everything that took place. That is not what we want. We want a change to policies so that they will not treat people like cattle. We are supposed to be a democratic nation and it is time our immigration policies reflected that fact. I hereby give notice that I intend to oppose every case of an individual against whom no criminal charge is pending-I am not talking of extradition cases, because that is a different category-being sent back to prison and to persecution behing the iron curtain.
Immigration is a privilege, not a right; we agree about that. But that does not mean that because people come here to seek admission they give up their rights as human beings. Yet that is the attitude of the department. It has got to come to an end. It has all the appearance of being a device to keep people out rather than to allow them in.
It may be that our complacement and arrogant attitude about immigration can be justified under present circumstances from a purely administrative point of view, but I am convinced that before too long this country will be out in the immigration market begging for people to come to Canada. And when we are, we will need all the goodwill we can get. We are not going about getting this goodwill in the right way. The last time I was in Europe I met a lot of people who complained bitterly about the attitudes and the approaches of our immigration policy. I hope something will be done to correct this.
I think we have got to do more to recognize the existence of young people in this country, not by giving out one-shot handouts, like the LIP program or Opportunities for Youth, but by creating a climate in which young people will see a consistent future for themselves in contributing to the expansion of the country in new fields of research and science, the opening of the north, or new industrial expansion.
There is confusion in the country, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) contributes to it when he goes to western Canada and accuses opposition members of contributing to alienation. He shows he just does not know what he is talking about. To us, Canada means freedom. It does not mean being placed in a little straitjacket designed by the bureaucrats in Ottawa. Nor does it mean accepting cultural programs designed by academics with a kind of hothouse approach that has no relationship to what people are thinking and feeling.
I am tired of hearing people say there is no Canadian culture and no Canadian identity. This is "bull fuzz", to use the kind of language the Prime Minister likes. Canadian identity is strong in western Canada and we do not

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Breau
need anyone to tell us what it is. Culture comes from people, not from some hothouse plant cultivated by government experts in government offices. There is more real Canadian culture in western Canada than in all the government departments and boards in Ottawa. When they learn that, then this government may be on the way to understanding some of the real facts of life in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise tonight to support the motion which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced and which reads as follows:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
The minister's budget is realistic, Mr. Speaker. It does not try to be dogmatic nor impose any economic philosophy. It comes to grips with the situation as it exists and deals with it in the most pragmatic way possible.

The opposition, of course, are saying that the budget is not much of an exercise in the proper management of the economy. I appreciate that it is their role to criticize, to oppose and, if necessary, to obstruct. But I am at a loss to understand the opposition parties when all they do is criticize and never suggest responsible alternatives. They say they have alternatives, but anyone can suggest alternatives and not mention the cost. I mean cost not only in dollars and cents but in the over-all effect of their proposals. All they do is try for the spectacular, the good-looking headline, and for narrow political purposes only.
The Conservative leader speaks of taxing Canadians on a constant dollar. To the ordinary Canadian who reads about this in the newspapers, it might sound pretty good; he might be led to believe that this is a practical approach. But he is not told by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfied) that for this to become a reality taxes will have to be increased each and every year, otherwise the economic power of the federal government will be eroded. Quite a bad thing to say for the leader of a party who advocates the concept of a guaranteed annual income, at a cost so high that he has not finished calculating it yet! Certainly, if he has, he has not told the people of Canada what the cost amounts to.
Neither has the ordinary Canadian been told that such a proposal would disrupt federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and make the estimates required so complex that it might ruin the have-not provinces. Quite a proposal for the leader of a party who is a former premier of a province and who preaches for more flexibility and better relations between the provinces and the federal government!
Nor has the ordinary Canadian been told that if this famous "constant dollar" concept should reduce the impact of the federal government in Canadian fiscal policy, it would mean that the efforts of the past and present to standardize basic social services in the country could not be continued. The role of the federal government as an equalizer would be minimized, as would its role in the field of regional development. Quite a thing to say for a maritimer, who like myself should be sensitive to the need of our area for more federal intervention to

improve our standard of living! To impair in any way the strength of the federal government would result in a economic disaster for the eastern provinces.
There is no question in my mind, having thought of the implications of the "constant dollar" concept, that the Leader of the Opposition was sincere when he suggested it, that all he was doing-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is more sincere than you are.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If he was sincere, then all I can say is that the Conservative party is bankrupt of ideas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He also knows more about it than you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish he did. If he was sincere in leading Canadians to believe that such a concept was consistent and compatible with our political system, then he must be bankrupt of ideas.
Then again we have the New Democratic Party floating from one idea to another during this debate. They are the believers in economic theology who are intellectually and politically isolated in this chamber. The one thing I regret about that party is that they have left the little man. They have forgotten about the disadvantaged, whether in terms of people or in terms of geography. The NDP is now becoming under its new leader-or old, I don't know which-the spokesmen of the bourgeois middle class. They are the proponents of universality in social programs, the supporters of programs which have not closed the gap between the haves and have-nots. I used to have a lot of respect for that party, whose members were often in the past called the social conscience of this chamber. I regret that to save their political skins they have abandoned that role to speak for the high-income labour class which pushes up costs in this country to the detriment of the more than 60 per cent of non-unionized workers, the working poor. And even worse, in respect of economic development policies they are becoming more and more the spokesmen of the Ontario-dominated Canadian business establishment, those who oppose regional development because it hurts their pockets in central Canada and because it creates competition for their products in the slow-growth areas.
How else can one explain the crusade of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) and the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) against the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, more specifically, the Regional Development Incentives Act. If they were speaking in any political constituency in the Maritimes or anywhere in eastern Canada, they would not have the guts to speak of such a thing. The truth of the matter is that the NDP believes in government control over everything. They will not admit that this would only perpetuate centralization in Canada. If they were honest in respect of their economic thesis they really would not believe in regional development. More bureaucracy, more control over the economy will only mean more for Ontario, which fortunately for them and unfortunately for the other regions of Canada, has become prosperous with nationalistic politics.
June 12, 1972

There has been a big change in the NDP. There has been a big change in the leadership of that party. It changed its leadership from one who was once premier of a province which had difficulties to one who is a member of the Toronto establishment. I can see why the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby would buy this but I do not understand how the hon. member for Regina East, who is from a disadvantaged area, could be such a sucker.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the only party which always sticks to the same social philosophy is the Social Credit Party. The only problem is the following: the Creditistes do not yet understand it and I will even add that they never could get anybody to understand it.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak about a much more important matter which concerns me more than the opposition parties, namely my constituency and northeastern New Brunswick. Hon. members will recall that last winter, on many occasions, there were demonstrations designed to draw the attention of all Canadians to the economic situation of that area. The federal-provincial FRED agreement has often been mentioned in this connection. That agreement has just been revised and renegotiated by the two levels of government, and it should be signed shortly.
I pointed out repeatedly to the House and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) that there was an almost total lack of flexibility in the administration of the agreement and that the lack of authority in the field contributed to making it more of a program that imposed a certain development to a group of people instead of a real program through which the resources of an area would be grouped, and the government services already there co-ordinated and improved, and above everything else the natural elements of progress taken advantage of in the area. Whether those elements are human, social, economic political or cultural, any development must encompass them all.
This also calls for the full participation of the people, as well as the commitment of every sector of society. I trust the new agreement soon to be signed will offer the people greater opportunities to particiapte in their own development.
I would like this evening, Mr. Speaker, to discuss three particular points concerning the efforts of the federal and provincial governments in northeastern New Brunswick.
I will deal in the first place with the need for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and other federal departments not to be satisfied in my area with the administration of the FRED agreement. A number of other economic sectors in northeastern New Brunswick require the special attention of federal departments. Fisheries are an example. Harbour development for deep-sea fishing in the Lameque, Shippegan, Caraquet and Lower Caraquet area is another. A more flexible policy, more closely directed to the construction of wharves for offshore fishing, especially in the Lower Gloucester area, is quite essential. Off-shore fishing today does not only represent a financial contribution for our area, it also has a social aspect.
The Budget-Mr. Breau
Transport will not be unduly affected by the FRED agreement, whether it be road building, railway service, or air transport. In fact, northeastern New Brunswick needs a much more rational and attractive policy concerning air transport service. Instead of subsidizing an inefficient service, we should favour the establishment of a jet service which would become profitable if airport facilities were centralized.
The FRED agreement must not either become a way out for the federal departments involved in northeastern New Brunswick.
The second point that I should like to raise is of great concern to me because it is related to a problem which may have nefarious social effects in the future. I am referring to the present political context in New Brunswick, to the political fact that this government has almost no members from northeastern New Brunswick. To this I add the lack of French representation in the provincial civil service. In fact, northeastern New Brunswick has fewer civil servants than the other regions of the province in Frederiction.
Even if we all want a political system more concerned with the establishment of priorities on an economical basis than with decisions of a purely political nature, when the time comes to decide upon programs or the allotment of government funds, one has to be realistic and think that the government will always protect its political interests. It may do so by taking more or less partisan decisions, but nevertheless a government must, if it wants to survive, satisfy its constituting elements.
We must remember that the FRED agreement signed in 1966 has brought to northeastern New Brunswick capital from the provincial government through the Equal Opportunities Program that come into operation on January 1, 1967.
In the same way as the federal equalization concept, this program equalized taxation in New Brunswick, as well as social services. It extended to northeastern New Brunswick services which has been inexistent for the past 100 years and direct results have been improvement of social services to the population, with secondary effects on the economy of the region.
This means that the FRED program, at that time, speeded up and intensified the development initiated by the then provincial government. As I understand it, that is the federal government concept of regional development: the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, together with the Department of Finance, through the equalization scheme, make resources available to provinces in order to intensify their development under a special agreement.
With this new FRED agreement, we have yet to see special efforts on the part of the provincial government, even though its own resources are reinforced by some $100 million from the federal government under the form of equalization payments intended to alleviate the economic problems of northeastern New Brunswick. Without such an injection from the provincial government the FRED agreement will be distorted by a conflicting philosophy about regional development between Ottawa and Fredericton.

The Budget-Mr. Breau
The FRED agreement should not be used to pay for any new project of the provincial government in northeastern New Brunswick. It was not so conceived by the federal government and I do not think it should. For the last few years the New Brunswick government not only at the political level but also at the administrative level, has had the habit, for any project in northeastern New Brunswick or as soon as the population exerts pressure to obtain something, of quite carefully looking up the FRED agreement for any available funds to meet those needs.
Clearly it means that the FRED agreement will be used to meet certain provincial expenses which should have been paid by the province anyway. And we should not forget that in addition to its own budget, which New Brunswick allocates in total freedom from federal influence, the province receives some $100 million from the federal government as equalization payments. In my opinion, it would be logical that most of these payments should be channelled toward northeastern New Brunswick because that region needs them most. Otherwise, the economic gap between northeastern New Brunswick and the rest of the province is going to widen instead of closing.
I noted with interest the statement that Premier Hatfield made recently in the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick to the effect that the province would commit itself to spend an additional amount of some $5 million under the FRED agreement. But do these $5 million actually represent an additional payment or the amount that the province expected to spend anyway as compared to what it spends elsewhere? It may well be that the provincial government appropriates $5 million for certain programs but what is the purpose of this if it spends $10 million in another area of the province to meet similar needs?
It is obvious that, over the past few years, no special effort has been made by the provincial government in the Northeastern part of New Brunswick with its own resources. There have been some efforts, but always under the FRED agreement. And I must add that the resources of the provincial government over which it has sole jurisdiction, include $100 millions in equalization payments from the federal government.
Approximately one year ago, the federal government announced a grant of $20 millions to the Province of New Brunswick for the construction of Highway 11, connecting Campbellton to Moncton. It appears that, because of this federal interference in an area of provincial jurisdiction such as highways, the province decided that the Northeastern part had already received its share for the next few years and that it would concentrate its own resources which, as I have said, include approximately $100 millions in equalization payments for the federal government and which are available for road construction in the other regions of New Brunswick. Therefore, I am asking what is the purpose of the federal government intervention in the building of Highway 11 if all it does is to make an expenditure that the province should have made anyway.
It seems to me that the province should have an annual budget of several million dollars for building highways. I feel that on top of the $20 million from the federal government, the province should spend far more than had been

allocated in its highway construction estimates for eastern New Brunswick as that area has the worst highways in the province-maybe in the whole country. In fact, it is the area in which the economy makes the building of new highways most essential.
I am most concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the conflict which seems to be developing between the federal government and the province of New Brunswick over the concept of regional development and of the FRED agreement with regard to northeastern New Brunswick. Unless that province uses its own resources, which will be increased through the FRED agreement, the gap between northeastern New Brunswick and the rest of the province is not going to decrease, but rather to become ever wider, for if one excludes from the general budget of that province statutory expenses related to education, welfare and hospitalization, that budget is only going to help develop other areas in New Brunswick.
The third point I want to raise concerns not only New Brunswick but also all provinces which have negociated special agreements with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
I have noticed in New Brunswick that when civil servants speak about development programs which are undertaken by both levels of government, they lack understanding of each other's viewpoint. I speak, of course, of civil servants of the federal governmant and of the provincial government.
I will take as an example the Community Improvement Corporation, called the CIC, an agency of the government of New Brunswick which is responsible for the administration of the northeast New Brunswick FRED agreement. The CIC, under its president Mr. Pat Blanchard, has to be one of the most responsive government organizations of which I have ever heard. Many people have criticized it, perhaps with justification. I also have criticized the CIC in the past. But the lack of results from the northeast agreement is not the fault of those who have administered it. The fault, rather, lies in the agreement itself, its rigidity, the lack of participation and involvement of the local people themselves at the conceptual stage. The fault does not lie with the CIC.
I take the CIC as an example, however, to demonstrate how difficult it is for a group of civil servants of one government to administer a program which involves also a group of civil servants on another level of government 800 or so miles away. The negotiations for the revised northeast agreement have been unnecessarily long because the two negotiating groups were not sufficiently sensitized to each others problems. The CIC civil servant in New Brunswick lives out the problems of northeastern New Brunswick. Most of the time he is born and educated there. But he does not know and does not appreciate how the federal government functions and, therefore, feels frustrated many times when he notes a stumbling block in some of his activities originating in Ottawa.
On the other hand, how does the DREE civil servant know about the way of life in New Brunswick? Sometimes for justifiable reasons, not very much. I have wit-
June 12, 1972

nessed hundreds of times conflicts between the federal government and the New Brunswick government which had nothing to do with the different politics of the two governments. The conflicts were neither due to difference in philosophy nor to lack of knowledge of the facts, but were merely conflicts of attitude between civil servants. This was not intentional, and often both sides were right.
However, one sometimes does not understand or appreciate what the other is planning or what he is thinking. It is impossible for a CIC civil servant in New Brunswick, for example, to grasp the policy intentions of DREE in northeastern New Brunswick after two, three or even 30 meetings. Even federal civil servants have to work here for many years before they really understand a policy of the federal government. On the other hand, it is impossible for a DREE official to grasp New Brunswick's policies and even less possible for him to appreciate the economic, social or cultural history of New Brunswick after a few visits or meetings in New Brunswick.
It is expedient that DREE implement a program of exchange of civil servants with the provinces with which it engages in special programs of development. Politicians can grasp policies faster because of the close relationship of political parties at all levels in Canada and because it is one's job in politics to continually study new policies and to read about them. However, a civil servant works in a specific field and more often than not it is too limited a field.
DREE officials should temporarily become civil servants of a province, and vice-versa, without a reduction in salary and with the least possible interference in their family lives. I am sure that even if it were done on a voluntary basis, a great number of provincial civil servants would take the opportunity of working with DREE for a period of time; and the same applies to DREE civil servants who would go on probationary work in some of the provinces as temporary provincial civil servants. I am sure that details as to the cost, because of the different salary scales of the different governments, as well as moving expenses could easily be worked out with the provinces.

For both sides, the benefit of such a program would be so huge that the extra expenses for either government would be readily justifiable.
Given the endeavours of this government in regional development, perhaps it would be only reasonable if it assumed the whole cost of such a program. I urge the government,, and especially the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, to earnestly study my suggestion and to discuss it with the provinces. Perhaps he could initiate an adequate pilot project in the northeastern area of the province, particularly under the FRED agreement.
An exchange between the officials of his department who were involved in the review of the FRED agreement and officials of the CIC might be quite profitable for those officials themselves and for both governments, and might bring closer together the federal bureaucracy and the citizens of my area.
Moreoever, the result cannot be anything but better understanding between all groups concerned. Federal
The Budget-Mr. Gleave
officials would understand provincial policies and, in turn, provincial officials could better understand and appreciate the federal policies.
I shall therefore conclude by asking the House to pass the motion introduced by the Minister of Finance that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government. As I said a while ago, the budget of the Minister of Finance is realistic and comes to grips with the present situation, and I hope that the House will adopt it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the last two speakers on the government side. Each paid some attention to the party of which I am a member in this House. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), if I am not mistaken, referred to us as the party which would give the government control over everything. That was at the start of his speech. At the end of his speech he pleaded that the federal bureaucracy could come closer to the people of his area. I say he had better pray that the two do not get closer to each other.
It's a laugh, Mr. Speaker. It is the ultimate in humour for a member or supporter of the government to harpoon any party in this House for attempting to exercise government control. At the present time, in the Standing Committee on Agriculture we are debating a bill which will permit the government to administer $150 million through the Farm Credit Corporation over a period of years, but the government refuses even to divulge to the committee its latest study of how that money will be spent. Somebody behind the curtain says that it may be because the government doesn't know itself. Let me tell the hon. member for Gloucester, for his edification, that when the government gets that bill bulldozed through this House, as it will in due time, a fair amount of that money will be spent in his province to adjust his farming community to what the bureaucracy in Ottawa think it ought to be. And if he thinks that will be a happy event, he should ask his neighbours in Prince Edward Island what they think of it, because they are the first victims of the whole lousy scheme.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not refer to that in my speech. You did not listen.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I listened. I can understand English, and when I put on the earphone I can understand the translation from the French. I am literate, Mr. Speaker; I even went to school. As I say, this has to be a big laugh.
The budget gave the biggest plums to big business. The government has created one of the biggest bureaucracies Ottawa has ever seen. When the hon. member talks about some future government creating a bureaucracy, I would point to what Charles Lynch, that enemy of the Liberals, recently wrote:
The Privy Council Office, which includes the Prime Minister's establishment and represents our equivalent to the White House in Washington-
I think that's a nice touch.
-goes up from $7.2 million to $10.8 million. This is more than the

The Budget-Mr. Gleave
$6.3 million it costs to operate the Senate, and it is gaining rapidiy-
This is what is happening to the present government bureaucracy, yet the hon. member talks about what we might do when we come to power.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There's no fear of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am well aware of the arrogance which habitually belongs to the Liberals. They think they have the God-given right to rule Canada forever. They have been around for a while, but I don't think they should consider themselves indestructible.
I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is not in the chamber at the moment. If he would like to have an assessment of how the people of western Canada view the budget, I suggest, that he read the Western Producer of May 18. The headline of its editorial was, "Budget ignores the farmer." That is a pretty fair assessment of the budget. It is true that the budget gives something to processors who are the people one step removed from the farmers, but the Western Producer points out that in effect the government is saying that if it gives enough concessions to industry, to the corporations, then all will be well. According to the Western Producer, the government is working on the trickle-down theory, which holds that if you put enough money up top it will trickle down to the people below. That is an old theory, Mr. Speaker. The only trouble with it is that generally it doesn't work.
The Western Producer says that the government would have got a lot more action and generated a lot more employment if it had injected significant amounts of money into the purchasing sector, which includes the farming community. Real purchasing power should have been given to the consumer sector, but instead the government stayed with the idea of giving concessions to the corporations, many of which are not even Canadian. Much of the savings which these corporations will make in reduced taxes on profits will go straight out of the country. In effect we will be subsidizing these companies and the subsidy will be leaving the country completely.
Another provision in the budget deals with accelerated write-offs. It provides a two-year write-off for depreciation on equipment bought for manufacturing or processing goods in Canada. I am a farmer; I have operated a business and I know something about what depreciation means. If someone gave me a two-year write off on the equipment I use on my farm, I would think it was one of the biggest tax breaks I could get. It is the next best thing to getting a hefty cut in your income tax rate.
The ordinary, everyday Canadian is paying for this kind of write-off. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) was crying about the small businessman. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that small businessmen, teachers, professional people, workingmen and their wives, whether they are on salary or hourly rated, and farmers are the people who will pick up the tab for the tax free concessions that are being given to big business. These are the people who will pay. I do not know how the government managed to justify this kind of approach, but I suppose by one means or another they will try to justify it to the people in addition to the concession that they have already given.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) enunciates policies in this House which are different from the approach he takes on the hustings. For instance, after it had been decided to pay a subsidy on hog production, this is what he said in Quebec when speaking on this question, according to an article in the Western Producer of February 17:
Agriculture will not be able to meet the challenge of the future if it does not become economically independent.
"Like any other industrial sector, it has to operate and will have to operate without subsidies, without outside aid, as a mature organism that has developed its full potential.
"It is becoming less and less acceptable that consumers bear the cost of farmers' deficiencies."
I wonder where the Prime Minister of Canada gets these ideas about the deficiencies of farmers. I wonder how long it took some of his experts to reach the conclusion that "Like any other industrial sector, it has to operate and will have to operate without subsidies, without outside aid . .An article in the Toronto Star of June 10 is headed "Logging threatens Quebec's environment". I do not know whether it does or does not, because I am not an expert in that field, but it struck me that in this area concessions have been given to International Telephone and Telegraph Company from both the federal and provincial governments. This article, written by Walter Stewart, reads in part:
As part of the incentive to encourage the deal, Rayonier is receiving $57.3 million in grants and loans from the federal government and the province of Quebec, along with the timber-cutting rights.
Mr. Speaker, $57.3 million from the two levels of government, while the Prime Minister stands in the same province and says that agriculture will be treated like any other industrial sector! I do not know whether the Prime Minister is trying to mislead the people of Canada or whether he does not know any better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Both.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is very hard to tell, at times. The article winds up by taking a very serious view of the whole development. I think hon. members on the other side of the House ought to know the serious view taken by the Western Producer, the spokesman for western agriculture, in respect of this kind of statement. The editorial of February 17 reads:
If, on the other hand, Mr. Trudeau believes what he said in Quebec, and sees it as future policy, all we can say is that February 2 was a bad day for Canadian agriculture, and at the same time a further alienation of the farm community. That, Mr. Trudeau may find, is something that Ottawa Liberals cannot afford.
That is the kind of reaction evoked in western Canada when the Prime Minister makes a speech in Quebec. Today we have television and radio, and so on. It is not like the days of Jimmy Gardiner and Mackenzie King when they could make one speech in Quebec and then go out to Saskatoon and make another. I think the Prime Minister had better realize that the time has come when these speeches are heard right across the country.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if the minister and hon. members on the other side of the House realize the effect
June 12, 1972

that fiscal policies they have been following have on our exports. We can see a decline in the price per bushel of wheat, barley, rapeseed and oats by just following the upward movement of the Canadian dollar. The fiscal policies of this government permit or encourage this increased value of the Canadian dollar, and it will have its effect in one of two ways: it will result in exports being curtailed or it will result in less income in the hands of the individual or company exporting the products whether primary or manufactured. Between May 23 and June 2 the effect of this policy on the price of barley was 1 i cents per bushel. That may not seem much to members across the way, but it means a lot to the man selling the product.
Mr. Speaker, this budget does nothing about foreign ownership. In fact, by reason of tax concessions I suspect that it tends to accelerate rather than retard the pace of takeover of Canadian companies by foreign companies. I found it rather shocking, that a few days ago a committee of this House decided to hold its meeting in camera while it made up its mind who it was safe to hear on the subject so that the Committee would not be unduly influenced. The press was unable to be present at that meeting. The Citizen, in an editorial today, wrote:
The Commons committee examining the foreign ownership bill was wrong to exclude the press from its first meeting. The action should not be repeated.
In another article on the same page, Charles Wheeler wrote:
More than half of Canada's manufacturing industry is American-owned, so is the whole of Canada's oil industry, almost all its motor industry, and perhaps most important, virtually the entire means of exploiting Canada's vast reserves of mineral wealth.
Yet this does not appear to concern the government unduly, Mr. Speaker. The article goes on to say: "The process goes on". The proposals which the government bring before the House are not taken seriously by the press of this country. The government of Saskatchewan became concerned, and is concerned about the takeover of land in that province and has taken steps to protect our heritage there.
Land is surely one of our basic resources. For three generations people have homesteaded and developed this land. We want to protect it and make sure it remains the property of Canadians. Our desire shocks and scares to death the cabinet minister for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Land). I suppose that is understandable because his frame of mind is the same as that of his colleagues who want to do nothing about this problem. For a long time I suspected that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt did not know too much about farming: I accept that because his whole education, his training has been in law. I thought he knew something about law, considering that he was dean of the faculty of law at a university.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not necessarily.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, he has commented on a provincial bill which is not an act. According to my information, this bill must go to committee; it will be examined and changes and alterations may be made to it and its approach. Before this has happened the minister has com-
The Budget-Mr. Gleave
mented on it. He has said, "Ottawa opposes it." He cannot wait to make his comments. He cannot wait until the clear, sharp outlines of the proposal emerge. He said that although there has been no formal communication with the Saskatchewan government, that government knows how the federal government feels.
The final sentence in the report before me says that the Saskatchewan bill has not been passed. This may be the first time that a minister of the federal government has taken a position on a bill before a province has enacted it into law. I suppose that is understandable in view of the way this government feels about foreign ownership. Apparently it welcomes it and hopes it will move in and take over larger chunks of our land and resources. The Minister of Justice said in the House, as reported at page 2353 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the bill has indeed been brought to my attention and I have sought comment on its constitutional validity. Although it is only in the bill stage, it does seem to me that if it is not unconstitutional it ought to be.
I am surprised that the minister at this stage should seek a ruling. Apparently he himself has already made one. If this government displayed half as much zeal in finding ways and means to protect the interest of Canadians so that at the end of this generation or perhaps the next Canadians could be assured that they would be master in their own house, it would be worth while.
I am not talking about our owning every tree in this country, every bit of beach, every bit of shore and every bit of cultivated land; I am talking about steps which are necessary and will make Canadians confident that they will be master in their own house. Let the government do that instead of, as it has to this time, running around and letting out screams of frustration and rage because a province is concerned and wants to protect its own resources. This concern is not peculiar to Saskatchewan. The government of Alberta is moving to protect Crown lands there. Prince Edward Island is concerned, Nova Scotia is concerned and Ontario is becoming concerned.
I wonder when the federal government will become concerned. If the minister I have referred to, or any of his cohorts think they can go to Saskatchewan in the next election and use this negative approach to carry them to victory, they will be the most disillusioned men who ever ran for office. The people of Saskatchewan know what is important and they have not forgotten the antics of men like Gardiner and Mackenzie King who tried to make all sorts of deals.
Before it is too late, let the present government take concrete action and make sure that the economy can provide for our people that well-being, material and spiritual, which it is capable of providing. The government is wrong when it says, "We must have so many jobs; let us leave it to the private sector to provide them." The hon. member for Fraser Valley East said we ought to be realistic. I am realistic. I do not expect private enterprise or business to act like a sugar-daddy. As a farmer, I do not behave like a sugar-daddy: I run a farm; I produce as well as I can and make as much as I can for myself and my family. If someone were to come along and say, "We want you to hire three more men," I would wonder who would pay them.

June 12, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
Let us be realists; let us be practical. It is not right to ask private industry to behave like a sugar-daddy. It is not right to put this load on private industry and say to it six months or one year from now, "You did not provide the jobs we need, therefore we are going to clobber you." This is the implication left by the government. Doing this job is the government's responsibility; it must not load somebody else with that task.
When government persists in acting in that fashion it abdicates some of its responsibilities. It is for the government to administer the financial and fiscal policies of this country. It must not turn its responsibility over to the private banks and then scourge them because they charge too much interest. It is up to the government to control interest rates in this country. That is their responsibility, and they are not discharging it. I think the members in my part of the House are realists. We know that Adam Smith is buried. I sometimes think those on the other side of the House still think he is walking around.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of reasons I am glad to take part in this debate. The first of those reasons is that I wish to congratulate the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), a young, active and devoted minister, who has proved that he could present a budget both sensible and serious, worthy of an excellent administrator.
Mr. Speaker, this debate also gives me an opportunity to list the priorities which must apply to the citizens of my constituency, and which in my opinion most of the citizens of Pontiac would support unanimously.
And when I talk about priorities, I do know what I am talking about because I came to know them through a questionnaire which I recently sent to all the families of my constituency.
The third question of that poll was the following:
What are the major problems facing Canada today?
And the 900 answers received from all parts of this vast constituency, comprising 60 municipalities in the three provincial ridings of Pontiac, Gatineau and Labelle, all pointed out to the following problems:
1.	Unemployment.
2.	Roads.
3.	No industries.
4.	No jobs.
5.	Social welfare.
It is therefore very easy to see that people are asking for jobs and an increased industrial development.
I agree with them and support their requests. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am always available to those who are interested in industry in my riding. Whenever, in my office here in this building, or at home over the week-end,
I meet with any officials of companies anxious to settle in my area, I do so with tremendous interest and in the hope that the action I am taking will result in creating the jobs that are so badly needed.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion is extremely important to us, and I am very happy to thank

its officials for having always given me their co-operation by accepting to meet with the businessmen who are looking for information on the grants available to industry in designated areas such as mine.
Unfortunately, applications for grants are not always accepted; but to this day several have been approved and several others are under consideration. We must not give up, and this is why I go on making representations to promote industrial development in my constituency.
Mr. Speaker, the House is certainly aware that the area which I represent went through a difficult period recently. I should like to emphasize something which has not received the attention it deserved, namely, the role of the ordinary citizen in my constituency. Every time a problem arises, be it floods in Fort Coulonge or its vicinity, or the closing down of plants in Maniwaki or Mont Laurier, the people of these communities are always ready to contribute their share in seeking solutions by joining in with study groups and task forces that are set up to deal with these problems.
I wish to commend the people in my constituency who have joined these citizens committees. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that a committee representing all our social classes can help in a concrete way to find solutions to the problems which concern us all.

There is no doubt that the Local Initiatives Program put forward by this government last winter has been an outstanding success nationally and locally in my own constituency. No less than $1,600,000 in projects was approved, creating approximately 1,000 jobs in 25 different municipalities in the constituency of Pontiac. There were, of course, many more good projects which unfortunately were not approved due to budget limitations. However, the over-all results were excellent, and I ask that the cabinet members consider seriously that this program be continued next year with even more funds allocated.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We often hear that too many unemployed persons are not willing to work. In so far as my constituency is concerned, that statement is very much untrue. I spoke to many of the project leaders and asked if they had encountered difficulties in finding personnel for their projects. In almost every case I was informed that the unemployed, when approached, were eager and willing to work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says there is a right not to work.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am talking about those who are willing to work. I am talking about residents in my constituency who have proven that the often heard statement that unemployed people are not willing to work is very much untrue.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have visited many of these projects and have been amazed at the ingenuity of the promoters. There were a wide variety of projects, including the
June 12, 1972

rebuilding of the old, historic wooden bridge in Mansfield township near Fort Coulonge, the one at Grand Remous, a handcraft centre at Maniwaki, an arena and swimming pool at Mont Laurier, many community halls and recreational projects such as snowmobile trails and day care centres.
The project in Shawville is also very interesting because it secured for this municipality the ownership of a fine old building which formerly housed the post office. When the postal department vacated the old building I was happy to co-operate with the Shawville council in contacting the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. As a result, the building was sold to the village of Shawville at a very reasonable price. Through a Local Initiatives Program grant, the council made a complete renovation of the building to accommodate the municipal offices, a meeting room and a public library. Further to this, an Opportunities for Youth grant was approved for a group of students from the area who wish to make a complete history of the district, and this will be housed in the new library.
These are some of the reasons I am a firm believer in this type of program. They involve the citizens of this country from coast to coast. This government deserves congratulation for its innovation and planning of these programs, including the highly successful Opportunities for Youth program. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country asked for government by participation, he got it. I am proud to serve with him and I hope we continue in this vein. There is a wealth of knowledge and skill in my constituency, and these programs have proved it. The people like government by participation and they want it to continue.
There have been many notable achievements in the past four years both on a national and a constituency level. We cannot rest on our laurels, however, and we, the members supporting this government, must continue our efforts on behalf of all Canadians. The new budget will result in increased pensions for our aged citizens in need of extra financial help and to other groups in need. Also of great importance is the fact that the measures announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) will instil new confidence into the business community, resulting in more and more jobs for Canadians.
The region I represent possesses great potential, especially in the tourist industry. Everyone knows, of course, of the skiing facilities in the Wakefield area of the Gatineau Hills which attract thousands of tourists all winter. The new development at Mont Ste. Marie is also becoming another major winter recreational facility. The federal government, through the National Capital Commission, has been involved for many years in the tourist industry through its continued development of Gatineau Park where many of my constituents have found employment. Leslie Park, a new development in the Otter Lake area, will also help bring many more tourists into Pontiac. There is also the well known provincial park, La Veren-drye, which is continually improving its facilities and attracting increasing numbers of visitors. All these facilities are becoming year-round attractions and will eventually provide continuous employment for an ever growing number of people.
The Budget-Mr. Lefebvre
Pontiac is one of the few unspoiled areas in eastern Canada readily accessible to major urban population centres. The development of Pontiac industrially must take place bearing in mind that our lakes, forests and streams must remain unpolluted, in which case the tourist industry also can develop bringing in thousands of visitors and creating jobs for our citizens. I have been in contact with NCC officials regarding the possibility of making part of that property in my constituency available to the Ottawa Zoological Society for the establishment of a zoo. Mr. Fullerton, the chairman of the NCC, replied to my letter informing me that this is to be done and brought to the attention of the persons responsible for choosing the site of this zoo. If such a facility were established in Pontiac, the development brought about in a wide area surrounding it would be fantastic.
Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament since 1965 I have learned increasingly to understand the problems of my constituents, working with them and for them. I have also learned to appreciate their suggestions and ideas, and together we have found solutions to some of these problems. In my opinion, this is the ideal way, the team work way. The citizens of Pontiac have ideas, aspirations and knowledge. They want their government and their representative to listen. This, I believe, has been done.
Another interesting project in which I have been involved is the effort to obtain recognition of old Fort William as a national historic site. This area of Pontiac county is rich in the history of the fur trading years, and I believe official recognition is deserved. The officials of the National Historic Sites and Monuments Board have replied to my letters informing me that they are at present studying the request. This area is not only of historical significance but it is one of the most beautiful along the Ottawa River. Its magnificent sand beach and towering pine trees could be developed into an outstanding tourist attraction. As far as I know, there are no official national historic sites in Pontiac, and I believe this one would be a natural choice as number one.

As I mentioned at the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, there were many problems in my constituency when I was elected for the first time and problems still exist. But the Pontiac citizens are aware of the tremendous efforts made by this federal government and their Member of Parliament in order to find a solution to those problems. I have always believed, Mr. Speaker, that a Member of Parliament must first of all serve his electors, that is why I keep travelling from one end of my constituency to the other so as to meet as many people as possible and offer to help them.
We have certainly improved the lot of Canadians since 1968, Mr. Speaker, the federal government's record with regard to the social measures that have been passed is very impressive.
When I was very young, Mr. Speaker, our parish priest used to say that paradise on earth does not exist, only in heaven will we find paradise. I often think of those words when I listen to members of other parties who are always criticizing and making unrealizable election promises.

June 12, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Canadian people are very well informed; they want a strong, realistic, responsible government, a government truly representative of the Canadian people, as the present government is.
Mr. Speaker, a political party which really wants to govern in a responsible manner must introduce measures for all Canadians: senior citizens, both young and not so young people, citizens from both rural and urban areas, members of both the working and the professional classes.
It is very important that we members of this House pass legislation designed to improve living conditions for all Canadians.
We must also take into account the fact that the budget of the Canadian government is that of all taxpayers, and that all citizens have to pay their share of it. A responsible government mustt bring down a realistic budget taking its priorities into consideration as well as all of the government expenditures. In my opinion, the present budget meets these criteria and most Canadians will endorse it.
In closing, I should like to emphasize the importance to my constituency of Bill C-5, an act to amend the Farm Credit Act, which would make it possible for the Farm Credit Corporation to make loans to facilitate the efficient operation of a farm rather than being tied to the more rigid rules laid down by the present act under which it must be proven necessary to operate the farm. There are many good farms in Pontiac. Some of the best dairy farms in eastern Canada are in operation there, and beef producers are also becoming increasingly important. I know some farmers who are rapidly approaching the age of retirement. They need an opportunity to secure loans so that younger men can take over.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has also stirred up interest by his recent statements about helping family farms so that the owner can enlarge his holdings or retire if he prefers. I am sure this legislation could bring benefit to my area, one in which farming is among the most important industries. Those engaged in it are honest, industrious and experienced. There are young men willing to take over if the opportunity is given them for a fair deal, which is all we are looking for.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-LAKK LOUISE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION FOLLOWING PUBLIC HEARINGS
NATIONAL PARKS-LAKK LOUISE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION FOLLOWING PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 311 questioned the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) on several points arising from the proposed village Lake Louise project.
[Mr. Lefebvre.J
Other questions have been asked in the House concerning this proposal. A public hearing has been held at which the views of various organizations and individuals were heard and recorded. To date, however, the minister has avoided giving any indication as to the government's decision with regard to the proposed village Lake Louise project.
At the outset I must say I am totally opposed to this type of commercial enterprise being allowed in our national parks. I am amazed that our national parks branch would even consider such a proposal. I am also amazed and upset that the minister in charge of our national parks system has not indicated his opposition to this type of commercialization which is entirely out of keeping with national parks objectives. It is almost unbelievable to think that any consideration would be given by the minister to a foreign-owned corporation, in this case Imperial Oil Limited, obtaining a foothold in our national parks system.
In October 1968 the minister made the following statement in a speech to the Canadian National Parks conference:
Our national parks are special places. They are dedicated, not to providing artificial sources of recreation and entertainment, but to preserving, for the benefit of present and future generations, significant natural features of our national heritage. They do not meet the over-all need for outdoor recreation space and they should not attempt to do so.
To do so would be to neglect the essential purpose of our present national park system-that is, the need to preserve parts of our environment in a natural, unspoiled state.
I endorse that statement, Mr. Speaker, and it certainly runs counter to the proposed building of the village Lake Louise project in Banff national park. We do not need the urbanization of our national parks, for this is what we are trying to avoid in park development. Our citizens should be able to enjoy the natural beauties of our parks without turning them into Coney Islands.
If we give way to the proposed commercialized project called village Lake Louise, then the very objectives and principles laid down for the preservation of part of our Canadian heritage for all time will be destroyed. It will be the start of a series of commercialized projects throughout our parks system. It should be stopped now. Let us at least give preference to quality of life and of the environment over the almighty dollar as far as our national parks system is concerned.
It is surprising that no thorough ecological impact study has been done by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development prior to the announcement of this proposal. To my knowledge these studies have never been made, yet they should be a requirement, especially for a project of this kind. Again, it is disturbing to think that those in control have ignored this very important aspect of conservation. This information is required before any consideration should be given to approval of the project. To my knowledge this survey has not been made. And if it has been made, it certainly was not made public at the hearings held several months ago.
