I might point out that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been rather lax, not only so far as our national parks' system is concerned but also in having adequate ecological studies made, for example in the James Bay and Arctic areas. We have seen a water-
June 12, 1972

ing down of land use permits in the north. This indicates to me that the department is more interested in the almighty dollar than in preserving the ecological balance in any part of the Canadian terrain.
I do not have much time left, Mr. Speaker, but in closing I should like to point out that Canadians generally would like to see a sharp extension of our national parks system. They would like to see more national parks spread throughout Canada. There are still several provinces without a sufficient number of national parks which would really protect the heritage of these provinces and of Canada.
But to return to the subject of village Lake Louise, we are not opposed to commercial enterprises of this nature being set up outside the park boundaries. There are many opportunities for those who wish to invest several million dollars in a topnotch ski project. This is where such a project should be built. Let us retain 100 per cent Canadian ownership of our park resources particularly insofar as village Lake Louise and Banff national park are concerned. Imperial Oil Limited, a foreign owned corporation, must be stopped from investing in this project.

speakeroldname: Mr. Allen B. Sulatycky (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-LAKK LOUISE PROJECT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT POSITION FOLLOWING PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the hon. member say he is in favour of a sharp extension in our national parks' system. The only thing he failed to say and to recognize is that in the past four years more national parks have been established in Canada than in the previous 50 years. We now have parks in every province and territory in Canada. Until this government came into power there were a number of provinces and territories which did not have national parks. I think a great deal of credit is due to the minister for this very sharp extension to our national parks system.
The hon. member, in his question of May 31, referred to evaluation of material gathered at the recent public hearings in respect of Lake Louise. I wish to deal with that aspect of his question. He went into the whole Lake Louise proposal. I could speak for a long time on that subject but I want to deal only with the matter he raised on May 31. The public hearing on proposals for the Lake Louise areas was the largest held to date in the series of public hearings that the national parks branch has held on national parks in Canada. We received 2,118 registered briefs plus more than 500 letters and other submissions which arrived after the deadline for official briefs. Including the transcript of presentations by 191 speakers at Calgary, the submissions and recommendations by the public total approximately 5,500 pages. This is a tremendous volume of material to review. However, we have assigned additional staff to the task of initial analysis, and the minister will soon be in a position to consider summaries and recommendations on some of the major issues.
As the minister stated on May 31, he still hopes to be able to inform the House before the summer recess of the government's decision. However, he wants to ensure that adequate consideration is given to the many reasoned and well documented submissions which were made by the public, including the recent views of the government of Alberta. I also want to point out that while many individu-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion als and organizations adopted a simple yes or no position on the proposals, others argued in favour of a variety of modifications. Our decision is not a simple one because some future course of action must be charted for the total Lake Louise area and there is a great range of alternatives to consider.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-OFFER OF GOOD OFFICES BY UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY GENERAL RESPECTING VIET NAM WAR-CANADIAN POSITION-REPRESENTATION TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
['Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has posed a number of questions but as we all know, I am restricted under Standing Orders to three minutes. Therefore I will attempt to deal with the major question, liaison with the private sector under the auspices of OFY.
The hon. member will appreciate that our liaison with the private sector to encourage participation in Oppor-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion tunities for Youth-type projects has necessarily been experimental. Our efforts to date have established three avenues of possible involvement by the private sector in this new employment style: one, shared-coast programs on projects of an entrepreneurial nature; two, referral of submitted OFY projects for complete funding by the private sector; and three, development of OFY-type programs by the private sector.
Both Shell Canada Ltd. and John Labatt Ltd. are participating in the shared-cost projects to create 39 jobs at a total cost of $18,500 to the government and $50,000 to the private sector. An example of this approach is a project in Victoria, British Columbia, to produce toys and playground materials specially adapted for use by exceptional children. Using $20,000 and donated materials, this project will supply hospitals and institutions with equipment valued at close to $100,000 and is viewed as a pilot operation for the possible development of a new industry for the Island.
John Labatt Ltd. is also experimenting with funding projects, which are referred to them by OFY, entirely by themselves. At a cost of $15,000 they have funded a project submitted by students of the University of Toronto business school to do management consulting for small businesses in the city. Finally, many companies have expressed interest in developing OFY-type programs within their own organizations. To date, only Dominion Textiles have done so, creating 28 project-oriented jobs filled by student applicants, at a cost of $40,000.
Thus our liaison with the private sector to date has created approximately 70 jobs with $125,000 committed by business. I must emphasize that each of the projects is highly experimental and is being closely followed by others in the private sector. We feel that the success of these initial projects will encourage others with whom we are presently consulting to participate themselves.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-OFFER OF GOOD OFFICES BY UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY GENERAL RESPECTING VIET NAM WAR-CANADIAN POSITION-REPRESENTATION TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 25 I asked the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) the following question:
In light of the initiative taken by the Secretary General of the United Nations in making available his good offices in the settlement of the regrettably escalating conflict in Viet Nam, can the minister advise the House whether the Canadian government was consulted on this matter and whether it is lending its support and encouragement to the Secretary General in his efforts toward bringing to an end this tragic and long continued conflict and, if so, have the views of this government been conveyed to the government of the United States?
Whereupon I received the usual answer given to spokesmen of this party when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) said:
I will take notice of that question on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Since then I have heard nothing of Canadian consultation or extension of good offices or good wishes. There are times when in this withdrawal phase of foreign policy there seems to be a determination on the part of the government to substitute wilful blindness for involvement or concern in ticklish international affairs and episodes. While, naturally, we can find many reasons for a comfortable detachment from the Viet Nam conflict, we cannot really insulate ourselves from its outfall both potential and actual. What this long-sustained war is doing to our most powerful ally and its world role cannot be brushed aside or ignored. Viet Nam has become a horrible albatross around the American neck, a grievous burden and an issue painfully divisive of the American body politic.
At the time the Secretary General made his offer there was widespread anxiety that a sharp and dangerous new level of escalation had been reached. The action of the President of the United States in ordering the new bombing of the north and blockades of the harbour of Haiphong was a dangerous move. So was the escalation of the ground fighting ordered and executed by the North Vietnamese. This regrettably came at a time when there at least seemed some reasonable prospect of the conflict winding down. Nor can we say that there is not still a grave and serious danger: as late as today the ominous rumble of thunder out of China could be heard.
While I fervently wish to see the United States disengage completely from its debilitating and painful role in Viet Nam, I do not belong to those who rail at the American role and cast upon Washington the full load of blame and responsibility. Others are fishing in troubled waters and the people of both Viet Nams continue to suffer and die. But the war cannot go on for one bruised and bitter

June 12, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion year after another. The awful suffering and terror must end. Therefore, we should welcome the proffered initiative of Secretary General Waldheim. We should welcome, too, any conciliatory moves among the great powers.
For this reason I believe we should all welcome the fact that the recent escalation did not prevent the President from carrying out what was seemingly a very useful series of meetings in the Soviet Union. No one believes that summitry is the answer to all our ills or the balm of all international tensions. Yet the over-all result of the American-Russian and the Sino-American meetings cannot be anything but beneficial in a day and age when reduction of world tension is an absolute essential.
I think the time has come, too, for us to look carefully at our ICC role. If there is nothing that can be done, there is nothing to be gained by retaining the pretence of value. In this area a move by the British and Russian co-chairmen for another general conference on IndoChina might be useful. But there seems to be reason for pessimism in this connection. The reasons are well known.
In this difficult and painful problem I assure the government that any useful effort it attempts toward peace will have the hearty and sympathetic support of the official opposition. I should also say that we must retain a distance between encouragement and disillusionment. Without that, we cannot proceed to any useful role in this tangled, painful and difficult international episode.

speakeroldname: Mr. lames Hugh Faulkner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-OFFER OF GOOD OFFICES BY UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY GENERAL RESPECTING VIET NAM WAR-CANADIAN POSITION-REPRESENTATION TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are undoubtedly aware, the difficulty affecting the possible involvement of the United Nations in the Indo China situation continues to be that neither of the parties most directly concerned, South Viet Nam and North Viet Nam, is a member of the world body, and North Viet Nam and its allies have always vigorously denied the authority of the United Nations to discuss the war in Viet Nam.
The new Secretary General of the United Nations is convinced, however, and the Canadian government shares his view, that this regrettable conflict can and should only be solved through negotiations. It was in this spirit that I understand Mr. Waldheim offered the good offices of the United Nations to all the parties concerned, on condition that all the parties concerned agreed to it. Unfortunately, as the Secretary General reported in an interview a few weeks ago, none of the parties gave any clear response to his offer.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) indicated in the House on April 26, Canada would be willing to co-operate with the Secretary General in any way that might be useful in order to promote the peaceful resolution of the Viet Nam conflict through negotiations. However, the question of whether an offer of good offices, including that made by the Secretary General, will be successful depends on whether the various parties agree to negotiations and are prepared to discuss the issues. Of course, a form for negotiations already exists in the Paris conference on Viet Nam where both public and secret talks have been held. We have favoured the return of the parties to the Paris conference but negotiations cannot be forced on them.
As has been said in the House before, there must be disposition to negotiate and there must be disposition to agree. As soon as there is any hope in this respect there may then be an opening for Canada or for the United Nations to make a helpful contribution. I can assure the House that in the meantime the Canadian government will persist in its efforts to promote the resolution of the conflict through negotiation.

subtopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-REJECTED APPLICATIONS-RESULTS OF SOLICITATION OF COMPANIES TO PROVIDE JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 31 I put a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) regarding the Opportunities for Youth program. I asked:
In view of the fact that the government has had a team calling on businessmen during the month of May to solicit private support for the opportunities for youth project applications turned down by the government, would the minister inform the House when he will publish the list of corporations that have agreed to participate in this plan?
At that time the minister said he would consider it, but he regretted to inform me that the list was not a long one. Today or yesterday I read an article, I believe in the Ottawa Citizen, which reported that a spokesman in the minister's department had said two companies had agreed to participate in picking up project applications. I cannot believe that there can only be two such companies, so I decided to raise the matter on the "late show" tonight. I believe the minister must be more successful than that. Also, today I noticed a report in the paper that Opportunities for Youth officials in Regina had talked to businessmen there, trying to encourage them to pick up Opportunities for Youth programs that had been turned down by the government.
Tonight I want to know more about this program, how many companies have agreed to participate in it, how many projects they have picked up and how many people will be employed. I would also like to know about the team that is going out to solicit support from corporations. How much is the department spending on this team and how many people are participating in it?
I think that in general the Opportunities for Youth program is basically and essentially a good idea. It is an idea that allows students to participate in creating something that they think is useful. But I do have many concerns about it. One of the chief concerns I have is shared by some hon. members opposite as pointed, out, I believe, in the Cohen report that was commissioned by the department. It said that last year most of the emphasis was placed on middle-class students, that most of the jobs went to those who could afford to go to university without student jobs, that these students were wealthy enough and could get by without Opportunities for Youth grants.
This is one of the criticisms of the program. It is very middle-class oriented. This is something the government should try to correct. For that reason I have suggested that an Opportunities for Youth or similar program should be started for non-student young people so that the young unemployed, the young workers, the young farmers could take advantage of such a program. This is one of

June 12, 1972

the recommendations the government should act upon if it is to make this program really relevant and meaningful to our young people.
I believe that in this year's Opportunities for Youth program only about 9 per cent of the participants are non-students. The rest are students. I suggest that this is a serious oversight. Also, the Opportunities for Youth program, in the way it is set up today, is a very short-term solution. Maybe it should be a continuing thing. The Opportunities for Youth program in many ways, for many young people is partly what they would call tokenism.
[DOT] <2220)
I would be glad if the parliamentary secretary would tell us what is going to happen to our university graduates. I noticed in the latest edition of the Financial Times an article which said that a lot of university students coming on the labour market this year are unable to find jobs. In 1965, corporations and companies were asking students to work for them, but now we find the reverse to be true and students cannot find jobs. The University of Toronto predicts that 25 per cent of the graduates will not be able to find employment, this despite the fact that many graduates will go back to university to continue their education.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary to elaborate on this part of the Opportunities for Youth program. How many companies are participating, how successful are they and what are the plans to approach large corporations?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has posed a number of questions but as we all know, I am restricted under Standing Orders to three minutes. Therefore I will attempt to deal with the major question, liaison with the private sector under the auspices of OFY.
The hon. member will appreciate that our liaison with the private sector to encourage participation in Oppor-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion tunities for Youth-type projects has necessarily been experimental. Our efforts to date have established three avenues of possible involvement by the private sector in this new employment style: one, shared-coast programs on projects of an entrepreneurial nature; two, referral of submitted OFY projects for complete funding by the private sector; and three, development of OFY-type programs by the private sector.
Both Shell Canada Ltd. and John Labatt Ltd. are participating in the shared-cost projects to create 39 jobs at a total cost of $18,500 to the government and $50,000 to the private sector. An example of this approach is a project in Victoria, British Columbia, to produce toys and playground materials specially adapted for use by exceptional children. Using $20,000 and donated materials, this project will supply hospitals and institutions with equipment valued at close to $100,000 and is viewed as a pilot operation for the possible development of a new industry for the Island.
John Labatt Ltd. is also experimenting with funding projects, which are referred to them by OFY, entirely by themselves. At a cost of $15,000 they have funded a project submitted by students of the University of Toronto business school to do management consulting for small businesses in the city. Finally, many companies have expressed interest in developing OFY-type programs within their own organizations. To date, only Dominion Textiles have done so, creating 28 project-oriented jobs filled by student applicants, at a cost of $40,000.
Thus our liaison with the private sector to date has created approximately 70 jobs with $125,000 committed by business. I must emphasize that each of the projects is highly experimental and is being closely followed by others in the private sector. We feel that the success of these initial projects will encourage others with whom we are presently consulting to participate themselves.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.26 p.m.
